title: Scalable testing of quantum error correction
summary: The standard method for benchmarking quantum error-correction is randomized fault-injection testing. The state-of-the-art tool \stim is efficient for error correction implementations with distances of up to 10, but scales poorly to larger distances for low physical error rates. In this paper, we present a scalable approach that combines stratified fault injection with extrapolation. Our insight is that some of the fault space can be sampled efficiently, after which extrapolation is sufficient to complete the testing task. As a result, our tool scales to distance 17 for a physical error rate of 0.0005 with a two-hour time budget on a desktop. For this case, it estimated a logical error rate of $1.51 \times 10^{-11}$ with high confidence.

AI.tldr: Scalable quantum error-correction benchmarking tool combining stratified fault injection with extrapolation to overcome limitations of randomized fault-injection testing for larger distances and low physical error rates.
AI.motivation: Randomized fault-injection testing using tools like stim becomes inefficient for benchmarking quantum error-correction at larger distances (beyond 10) and low physical error rates, requiring a more scalable approach.
AI.method: Combines stratified fault injection with extrapolation: efficiently samples parts of the fault space and uses extrapolation to complete the testing task, enabling scalable benchmarking.
AI.result: Tool scales to distance 17 for physical error rate 0.0005 within 2 hours on a desktop, estimating logical error rate of 1.51×10⁻¹¹ with high confidence.
AI.conclusion: The stratified fault injection with extrapolation approach provides a scalable solution for benchmarking quantum error-correction at larger distances and low physical error rates where current methods fail.

title: Agnostic Parameter Estimation with Large Spins
summary: The quantum Fisher information of a quantum state with respect to a certain parameter quantifies the sensitivity of the quantum state to changes in that parameter. Maximizing the quantum Fisher information is essential for achieving the optimal estimation precision of quantum sensors. A typical quantum sensor involves a qubit(e.g. a spin-1/2) probe undergoing an unknown rotation, here the unknown rotation angle is the parameter to be estimated. A well known limitation is that if the rotation axis is unknown, the maximal quantum Fisher information is impossible to attain. This limitation has been lifted recently by leveraging entanglement between the probe qubit and an ancilla qubit. Namely, through measurement of the ancilla after the axis is revealed, one can prepare the probe that is optimal for any unknown rotation axis. This proposal, however, works only for a spin-1/2. Considering large spin probes can achieve a larger quantum Fisher information, offering enhanced metrological advantage, we here utilize the entanglement between a large spin probe and an ancilla to achieve optimal quantum Fisher information for estimating the rotation angle, without prior knowledge of the rotation axis. Different from the previous spin-1/2 case, achieving the optimal precision with large spins generally requires post-selection, resulting in a success probability dependent on the dimension of the Hilbert space. Furthermore, we extend the encoding state from the maximally entangled case to general entangled states, showing that optimal metrology can still be achieved with a certain success probability.

AI.tldr: Large spin probes entangled with ancillas enable optimal quantum Fisher information for rotation angle estimation without prior knowledge of rotation axis, overcoming limitations of spin-1/2 systems.
AI.motivation: Traditional quantum sensors face limitations when the rotation axis is unknown - maximal quantum Fisher information cannot be attained. While entanglement between spin-1/2 probes and ancillas recently overcame this limitation, large spin probes offer greater quantum Fisher information and enhanced metrological advantages, motivating extension to large spin systems.
AI.method: Utilize entanglement between a large spin probe and an ancilla qubit. After the unknown rotation axis is revealed, measure the ancilla to prepare the probe in an optimal state for any rotation axis. The approach requires post-selection for large spins, with success probability dependent on Hilbert space dimension. Extend from maximally entangled states to general entangled states.
AI.result: Optimal quantum Fisher information for rotation angle estimation can be achieved without prior knowledge of rotation axis using large spin probes entangled with ancillas. Unlike spin-1/2 case, optimal precision with large spins requires post-selection, with success probability scaling with Hilbert space dimension. Optimal metrology can also be achieved with general entangled states, not just maximally entangled ones.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement between large spin probes and ancillas enables optimal quantum metrology for rotation angle estimation without axis knowledge, overcoming fundamental limitations of spin-1/2 systems and offering enhanced metrological advantages through larger quantum Fisher information.

title: Instance-optimal high-precision shadow tomography with few-copy measurements: A metrological approach
summary:
We study the sample complexity of shadow tomography in the high-precision regime under realistic measurement constraints. Given an unknown $d$-dimensional quantum state $ρ$ and a known set of observables $\{O_i\}_{i=1}^m$, the goal is to estimate expectation values $\{\mathrm{tr}(O_iρ)\}_{i=1}^m$ to accuracy $ε$ in $L_p$-norm, using possibly adaptive measurements that act on $O(\mathrm{polylog}(d))$ number of copies of $ρ$ at a time. We focus on the regime where $ε$ is below an instance-dependent threshold.
  Our main contribution is an instance-optimal characterization of the sample complexity as $\tildeΘ(Γ_p/ε^2)$, where $Γ_p$ is a function of $\{O_i\}_{i=1}^m$ defined via an optimization formula involving the inverse Fisher information matrix. Previously, tight bounds were known only in special cases, e.g. Pauli shadow tomography with $L_\infty$-norm error. Concretely, we first analyze a simpler oblivious variant where the goal is to estimate an observable of the form $\sum_{i=1}^m α_i O_i$ with $\|α\|_q = 1$ (where $q$ is dual to $p$) revealed after the measurement. For single-copy measurements, we obtain a sample complexity of $Θ(Γ^{\mathrm{ob}}_p/ε^2)$. We then show $\tildeΘ(Γ_p/ε^2)$ is necessary and sufficient for the original problem, with the lower bound applying to unbiased, bounded estimators. Our upper bounds rely on a two-step algorithm combining coarse tomography with local estimation. Notably, $Γ^{\mathrm{ob}}_\infty = Γ_\infty$. In both cases, allowing $c$-copy measurements improves the sample complexity by at most $Ω(1/c)$.
  Our results establish a quantitative correspondence between quantum learning and metrology, unifying asymptotic metrological limits with finite-sample learning guarantees.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes instance-optimal sample complexity bounds for shadow tomography in the high-precision regime under realistic measurement constraints, showing it scales as $\tildeΘ(Γ_p/ε^2)$ where $Γ_p$ is an instance-dependent quantity defined via Fisher information optimization.
AI.motivation: Previous tight bounds for shadow tomography were known only in special cases (e.g., Pauli shadow tomography with $L_∞$-norm error). The paper aims to characterize the sample complexity in the high-precision regime under realistic constraints where measurements act on only $O(\mathrm{polylog}(d))$ copies at a time, focusing on the regime where accuracy $ε$ is below an instance-dependent threshold.
AI.method: The authors first analyze an oblivious variant where the goal is to estimate an observable of the form $\sum_{i=1}^m α_i O_i$ with $\|α\|_q = 1$ revealed after measurement. For single-copy measurements, they obtain sample complexity $Θ(Γ^{\mathrm{ob}}_p/ε^2)$. They then show $\tildeΘ(Γ_p/ε^2)$ is necessary and sufficient for the original problem, with lower bounds applying to unbiased, bounded estimators. Upper bounds use a two-step algorithm combining coarse tomography with local estimation.
AI.result: The main result is an instance-optimal characterization of sample complexity as $\tildeΘ(Γ_p/ε^2)$, where $Γ_p$ is defined via an optimization formula involving the inverse Fisher information matrix. Notably, $Γ^{\mathrm{ob}}_∞ = Γ_∞$, and allowing $c$-copy measurements improves sample complexity by at most $Ω(1/c)$.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a quantitative correspondence between quantum learning and metrology, unifying asymptotic metrological limits with finite-sample learning guarantees. The work provides tight bounds for shadow tomography under realistic measurement constraints in the high-precision regime.

title: Efficient time-evolution of matrix product states using average Hamiltonians
summary: Simulating quantum many-body systems (QMBS) is one of the long-standing, highly non-trivial challenges in condensed matter physics and quantum information due to the exponentially growing size of the system's Hilbert space. To date, tensor networks have been an essential tool for studying such quantum systems, owing to their ability to efficiently capture the entanglement properties of the systems they represent. One of the well-known tensor network architectures, namely matrix product states (MPS), is the standard method for simulating one-dimensional QMBS. Here, we propose a simple, yet efficient, method to augment the already available MPS algorithms to simulate the dynamics of time-dependent Hamiltonians with better accuracy and a faster convergence rate, giving a second-order convergence compared to the first-order convergence of the standard method. We apply our proposed method to simulate the dynamics of a chain of single spins associated with nitrogen-vacancy color centers in diamonds, which has potential applications for practical and scalable quantum technologies, and find that our method improves the average error for a system of few NV centers by a factor of about 1000 for moderate step sizes. Our work paves the way for efficient simulation of QMBS under the influence of time-dependent Hamiltonians.

AI.tldr: Proposed method enhances MPS algorithms for simulating time-dependent quantum many-body systems with second-order convergence, achieving ~1000x error reduction for NV center spin chains.
AI.motivation: Simulating quantum many-body systems is challenging due to exponential Hilbert space growth. While MPS is standard for 1D systems, existing methods for time-dependent Hamiltonians have only first-order convergence, limiting accuracy and efficiency.
AI.method: Augments existing MPS algorithms with a simple yet efficient approach to simulate dynamics of time-dependent Hamiltonians, achieving second-order convergence compared to standard first-order methods.
AI.result: Method improves average error by factor of ~1000 for moderate step sizes when simulating NV center spin chains. Demonstrates better accuracy and faster convergence rate for time-dependent Hamiltonian simulations.
AI.conclusion: Proposed augmentation paves way for efficient simulation of quantum many-body systems under time-dependent Hamiltonians, with significant error reduction and improved convergence properties.

title: Heterogeneity dominates irreversibility in random Markov models
summary: We introduce a two-parameter ensemble of random discrete-time Markov models that simultaneously captures critical slowing down and broken detailed balance. Extending a previously studied heterogeneous Markov ensemble, we incorporate correlations between forward and backward transition rates through a single asymmetry parameter $γ$, while heterogeneity is controlled by $ε$. Using results from random matrix theory, we identify a critical locus $ε_c(γ,N)$ at which relaxation times diverge and spectral universality breaks down. We characterize the behavior of entropy production, predictive information, and relaxation dynamics across the ensemble, showing that many observables depend strongly on heterogeneity but only weakly on asymmetry, except near the symmetric limit. Applying maximum-likelihood inference to human fMRI and EEG data, we find that both modalities operate near the predicted critical locus and occupy a similar region of the $ε-γ$ plane, supporting a super-universality of human brain dynamics. While ensemble averages are well captured by the null model, empirical data exhibit substantially enhanced variability, indicating subject-specific structure beyond random expectations. Our results unify criticality and nonequilibrium measures within a single framework and clarify their intertwined role in the analysis of complex biological dynamics.

AI.tldr: Two-parameter random Markov ensemble captures critical slowing down and broken detailed balance, revealing super-universality in human brain dynamics near predicted critical locus.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified framework that simultaneously captures critical slowing down and broken detailed balance in complex biological dynamics, particularly to understand the intertwined role of criticality and nonequilibrium measures in systems like human brain activity.
AI.method: Introduce a two-parameter ensemble of random discrete-time Markov models with parameters γ controlling asymmetry (correlations between forward/backward rates) and ε controlling heterogeneity. Use random matrix theory to identify critical locus ε_c(γ,N) where relaxation times diverge. Characterize entropy production, predictive information, and relaxation dynamics. Apply maximum-likelihood inference to human fMRI and EEG data.
AI.result: Identified critical locus where relaxation times diverge and spectral universality breaks down. Found that observables depend strongly on heterogeneity but weakly on asymmetry except near symmetric limit. Human fMRI and EEG data operate near predicted critical locus and occupy similar region in ε-γ plane, supporting super-universality of brain dynamics. Empirical data show enhanced variability beyond random expectations.
AI.conclusion: The framework unifies criticality and nonequilibrium measures, clarifying their intertwined role in complex biological dynamics. Human brain dynamics exhibit super-universality near critical locus while maintaining subject-specific structure beyond random expectations.

title: Topological frustration and quantum resources
summary: Although in general boundary conditions do not affect the bulk properties of a system, some of them are special and defy such expectation. This is the case, for instance, of those inducing geometrical frustration in a classical magnet. Recently, the study of such settings in quantum systems (dubbed topological frustration) has uncovered peculiar features, interesting both from a fundamental and technological point of view. In this work, we present and discuss the behavior of several quantum resources in presence of TF, namely the (disconnected) entanglement entropy and the non-stabilizerness Renyi entropy. We will show that, compared to their non-frustrated counterparts, TF adds a distinct contribution to these resources, due to a stable, delocalized, topological excitation. Remarkably, this contribution can be calculated analytically, due to its similarities with that of a W-state.

AI.tldr: Topological frustration in quantum systems adds distinct contributions to entanglement entropy and non-stabilizerness Renyi entropy due to stable delocalized topological excitations, analogous to W-states.
AI.motivation: To investigate how topological frustration (special boundary conditions that defy conventional expectations) affects quantum resources like entanglement entropy and non-stabilizerness Renyi entropy, building on recent studies showing topological frustration creates peculiar features with fundamental and technological significance.
AI.method: Analysis of quantum systems with topological frustration, examining the behavior of disconnected entanglement entropy and non-stabilizerness Renyi entropy, comparing them with non-frustrated counterparts, and identifying contributions from stable delocalized topological excitations.
AI.result: Topological frustration adds distinct contributions to quantum resources that can be calculated analytically due to similarities with W-states, revealing stable delocalized topological excitations that persist in these systems.
AI.conclusion: Topological frustration introduces measurable, analytically calculable contributions to quantum entanglement and non-stabilizerness metrics through stable topological excitations, offering insights into quantum resource manipulation and potential technological applications.

title: Beyond overcomplication: a linear model suffices to decode hidden structure-property relationships in glasses
summary: Establishing reliable and interpretable structure-property relationships in glasses is a longstanding challenge in condensed matter physics. While modern data-driven machine learning techniques have proven highly effective in establishing structure-property correlations, many models are criticized for lacking physical interpretability and being task-specific. In this work, we identify an approximate linear relation between structure profiles and disorder-induced responses of glass properties based on first order perturbation theory. We analytically demonstrate that this relationship holds universally across glassy systems with varying dimensions and distinct interaction types. This robust theoretical relationship motivates the adoption of linear machine learning models, which we show numerically to achieve surprisingly high predictive accuracy for structure-property mapping in a wide variety of glassy materials. We further devise regularization analysis to further enhance the interpretability of our model, bridging the gap between predictive performance and physical insight. Overall, this linear relation establishes a simple yet powerful connection between structural disorder and spectral properties in glasses, opening a new avenue for advancing their studies.

AI.tldr: The paper discovers a universal linear relationship between structural disorder profiles and property responses in glasses, enabling interpretable linear ML models with high predictive accuracy.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of establishing reliable and interpretable structure-property relationships in glasses, overcoming limitations of current data-driven ML models that lack physical interpretability and are task-specific.
AI.method: Based on first-order perturbation theory, the authors identify an approximate linear relation between structure profiles and disorder-induced property responses. They analytically demonstrate this relationship's universality across glassy systems with varying dimensions and interaction types, then implement linear machine learning models with regularization analysis to enhance interpretability.
AI.result: The linear relationship holds universally across diverse glassy systems. Linear ML models achieve surprisingly high predictive accuracy for structure-property mapping in various glassy materials. Regularization analysis further enhances model interpretability while maintaining predictive performance.
AI.conclusion: The discovered linear relation establishes a simple yet powerful connection between structural disorder and spectral properties in glasses, bridging the gap between predictive performance and physical insight, and opening new avenues for advancing glass studies.

title: Tighter Asymptotic Key Rates for Intensity-Correlated Decoy-State QKD via Nonlinear Programming
summary: Decoy-state QKD with phase-randomized weak coherent pulses is typically analyzed assuming independent, precisely prepared intensities. Real sources, however, can exhibit correlated intensity drift across rounds, potentially leaking intensity information and breaking the standard decoy-state reduction to linear programs. Cauchy--Schwarz (CS) constraints can restore security by coupling $n$-photon yields across intensities, but they introduce nonlinear square-root constraints that are commonly handled via outer linearisation around channel-model-based reference points. We propose a reproducible alternative: first solve the full CS-constrained parameter-estimation problems using the interior-point nonlinear solver IPOPT, then use the resulting candidate solution as the linearisation point for the outer optimisation that certifies a valid lower bound on the asymptotic key rate. Simulations for both coarse-grained model-independent correlations and fine-grained truncated-Gaussian models show consistently tighter key-rate bounds than canonical reference points, and in some cases allow certifying optimality when both optimisation stages coincide.

AI.tldr: Proposes a reproducible method for decoy-state QKD with intensity correlations: solve full CS-constrained problem with IPOPT, then use solution as linearization point for outer optimization to certify valid key-rate lower bounds.
AI.motivation: Real quantum key distribution sources exhibit correlated intensity drift across rounds, which leaks intensity information and breaks standard decoy-state reduction to linear programs. Current methods using Cauchy-Schwarz constraints introduce nonlinear constraints that are typically handled via linearization around channel-model-based reference points, which may not be optimal.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: 1) Solve the full Cauchy-Schwarz constrained parameter-estimation problems using interior-point nonlinear solver IPOPT to obtain candidate solution, 2) Use this solution as the linearization point for the outer optimization that certifies a valid lower bound on the asymptotic key rate.
AI.result: Simulations for both coarse-grained model-independent correlations and fine-grained truncated-Gaussian models show consistently tighter key-rate bounds than canonical reference points. In some cases, the method allows certifying optimality when both optimization stages coincide.
AI.conclusion: The proposed reproducible method provides tighter security bounds for decoy-state QKD with intensity correlations by using solutions from full nonlinear optimization as linearization points, outperforming traditional channel-model-based reference points.

title: The weak and strong disorder regimes in the continuous random field Ising model
summary: We present a nonperturbative analysis of the weak- and strong-disorder regimes of the continuous random-field Ising model using the distributional zeta-function method. By performing the quenched-disorder average at the level of the effective action, we derive exact quadratic and interaction terms. In the weak-disorder limit, we show that the infrared structure of the two-point correlation functions yields a decomposition of the physical field into correlated components with distinct scaling dimensions. This mechanism exhibits the characteristic $1/p^4$ behavior, which shifts the upper critical dimension to $d_c^{+}=6$. The universal critical behavior of the RFIM near this dimension is governed by a minimal infrared effective action. In the strong-disorder regime, we obtain an exact diagonal quadratic action with a discrete spectrum of massive modes. Here, the absence of massless modes implies the absence of conventional criticality. The resulting spectral representation of correlation functions converges rapidly and remains well controlled in the infrared regime.

AI.tldr: Nonperturbative analysis of random-field Ising model using distributional zeta-function method reveals distinct weak- and strong-disorder regimes with different critical behaviors and dimensional shifts.
AI.motivation: To provide a nonperturbative understanding of the continuous random-field Ising model (RFIM) across different disorder regimes using rigorous mathematical methods that avoid perturbative approximations.
AI.method: Distributional zeta-function method applied to quenched-disorder average at the effective action level, deriving exact quadratic and interaction terms for both weak- and strong-disorder limits.
AI.result: In weak disorder: infrared structure shows field decomposition into correlated components with distinct scaling dimensions, exhibiting 1/p^4 behavior shifting upper critical dimension to d_c^+=6. In strong disorder: exact diagonal quadratic action with discrete massive spectrum, no massless modes, and well-controlled infrared convergence.
AI.conclusion: The RFIM exhibits fundamentally different behaviors in weak vs strong disorder regimes - weak disorder shows conventional criticality with shifted upper critical dimension, while strong disorder lacks conventional criticality due to absence of massless modes, with both regimes having well-controlled infrared properties.

title: Taming multiparty entanglement at measurement-induced phase transitions
summary: Measurement-induced phase transitions (MIPT) give rise to novel dynamical states of quantum matter realized by balancing unitary evolution and measurements. We present large-scale numerical simulations of a trapped-ion native MIPT, argued to belong to the universality class described by the Haar non-unitary conformal field theory. First, through a finite-size analysis we obtained the critical measurement rate, and correlation length exponent, which falls close to the percolation value. Second, by leveraging a monotone computable via semi-definite programming, we uncover robust algebraic decay of genuine multiparty entanglement (GME) versus separation for 2, 3, and 4 parties. The corresponding critical exponents are lower-bounded by those of the multiparty mutual information, which we determine up to 4 parties, and conjecture to be (k+2) for k parties. Additionally, we derive lower bounds for both GME and multiparty mutual information.

AI.tldr: Numerical study of measurement-induced phase transitions in trapped-ion systems reveals critical exponents near percolation values and algebraic decay of genuine multiparty entanglement with conjectured scaling of (k+2) for k-party mutual information.
AI.motivation: To investigate measurement-induced phase transitions (MIPT) in trapped-ion systems and characterize their universal properties, particularly the critical behavior and multiparty entanglement scaling at the transition point.
AI.method: Large-scale numerical simulations of trapped-ion native MIPT, finite-size analysis to extract critical parameters, and use of semi-definite programming to compute monotones for analyzing genuine multiparty entanglement decay.
AI.result: Critical measurement rate and correlation length exponent close to percolation value; robust algebraic decay of genuine multiparty entanglement for 2, 3, and 4 parties; lower bounds for GME and multiparty mutual information; conjecture that k-party mutual information critical exponent scales as (k+2).
AI.conclusion: The trapped-ion MIPT belongs to the Haar non-unitary CFT universality class, exhibits percolation-like critical exponents, and displays characteristic algebraic decay of multiparty entanglement with conjectured scaling relationships.

title: Distributed Quantum Error Mitigation: Global and Local ZNE encodings
summary: Errors are the primary bottleneck preventing practical quantum computing. This challenge is exacerbated in the distributed quantum computing regime, where quantum networks introduce additional communication-induced noise. While error mitigation techniques such as Zero Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) have proven effective for standalone quantum processors, their behavior in distributed architectures is not yet well understood. We investigate ZNE in this setting by comparing Global optimization (ZNE is applied prior to circuit partitioning), against Local optimization (ZNE is applied independently to each sub-circuit). Partitioning is performed on a monolithic circuit, which is then transformed into a distributed implementation by inserting noisy teleportation-based communication primitives between sub-circuits. We evaluate both approaches across varying numbers of quantum processing units (QPUs) and under heterogeneous local and network noise conditions. Our results demonstrate that Global ZNE exhibits superior scalability, achieving error reductions of up to $48\%$ across six QPUs. Moreover, we observe counterintuitive noise behavior, where increasing the number of QPUs improves mitigation effectiveness despite higher communication overhead. These findings highlight fundamental trade-offs in distributed quantum error mitigation and raise new questions regarding the interplay between circuit structure, partitioning strategies, and network noise.

AI.tldr: Global ZNE optimization outperforms Local ZNE in distributed quantum computing, achieving up to 48% error reduction across 6 QPUs, with counterintuitive noise behavior where more QPUs improve mitigation despite higher communication overhead.
AI.motivation: Errors are the primary bottleneck in quantum computing, exacerbated in distributed architectures where network communication introduces additional noise. While Zero Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) works for standalone processors, its behavior in distributed quantum computing is not well understood.
AI.method: Investigate ZNE in distributed quantum computing by comparing Global optimization (ZNE applied before circuit partitioning) against Local optimization (ZNE applied independently to each sub-circuit). Partition monolithic circuits and insert noisy teleportation-based communication primitives between sub-circuits. Evaluate across varying numbers of QPUs under heterogeneous local and network noise conditions.
AI.result: Global ZNE exhibits superior scalability with error reductions up to 48% across six QPUs. Counterintuitive noise behavior observed: increasing QPU count improves mitigation effectiveness despite higher communication overhead. Results highlight trade-offs in distributed quantum error mitigation.
AI.conclusion: Global ZNE optimization is more effective than Local ZNE for distributed quantum computing. Findings reveal fundamental trade-offs in distributed error mitigation and raise new questions about the interplay between circuit structure, partitioning strategies, and network noise.

title: Quantum-Inspired Algorithm for Classical Spin Hamiltonians Based on Matrix Product Operators
summary: We propose a tensor-network (TN) approach for solving classical optimization problems that is inspired by spectral filtering and sampling on quantum states. We first shift and scale an Ising Hamiltonian of the cost function so that all eigenvalues become non-negative and the ground states correspond to the the largest eigenvalues, which are then amplified by power iteration. We represent the transformed Hamiltonian as a matrix product operator (MPO) and form an immense power of this object via truncated MPO-MPO contractions, embedding the resulting operator into a matrix product state for sampling in the computational basis. In contrast to the density-matrix renormalization group, our approach provides a straightforward route to systematic improvement by increasing the bond dimension and is better at avoiding local minima. We also study the performance of this power method in the context of a higher-order Ising Hamiltonian on a heavy-hexagonal lattice, making a comparison with simulated annealing. These results highlight the potential of quantum-inspired algorithms for solving optimization problems and provide a baseline for assessing and developing quantum algorithms.

AI.tldr: Tensor-network approach using power iteration and MPO representation to solve classical optimization problems, outperforming DMRG and simulated annealing in avoiding local minima.
AI.motivation: Develop quantum-inspired tensor-network algorithms for classical optimization that can systematically improve performance and avoid local minima better than existing methods like DMRG and simulated annealing.
AI.method: Transform Ising Hamiltonian via shift/scale to make eigenvalues non-negative, apply power iteration to amplify ground states, represent as MPO, compute high powers via truncated MPO-MPO contractions, and sample from resulting matrix product state.
AI.result: The approach provides systematic improvement by increasing bond dimension, better avoids local minima than DMRG, and shows competitive performance against simulated annealing on heavy-hexagonal lattice Ising models.
AI.conclusion: Tensor-network power methods offer promising quantum-inspired algorithms for optimization, establishing baselines for quantum algorithm development and assessment.

title: QuantumGS: Quantum Encoding Framework for Gaussian Splatting
summary: Recent advances in neural rendering, particularly 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), have enabled real-time rendering of complex scenes. However, standard 3DGS relies on spherical harmonics, which often struggle to accurately capture high-frequency view-dependent effects such as sharp reflections and transparency. While hybrid approaches like Viewing Direction Gaussian Splatting (VDGS) mitigate this limitation using classical Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), they remain limited by the expressivity of classical networks in low-parameter regimes. In this paper, we introduce QuantumGS, a novel hybrid framework that integrates Variational Quantum Circuits (VQC) into the Gaussian Splatting pipeline. We propose a unique encoding strategy that maps the viewing direction directly onto the Bloch sphere, leveraging the natural geometry of qubits to represent 3D directional data. By replacing classical color-modulating networks with quantum circuits generated via a hypernetwork or conditioning mechanism, we achieve higher expressivity and better generalization. Source code is available in the supplementary material. Code is available at https://github.com/gwilczynski95/QuantumGS

AI.tldr: QuantumGS integrates variational quantum circuits into 3D Gaussian Splatting to better capture high-frequency view-dependent effects by mapping viewing directions onto the Bloch sphere and replacing classical networks with quantum circuits.
AI.motivation: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting struggles with high-frequency view-dependent effects like sharp reflections and transparency using spherical harmonics, and existing hybrid approaches using classical MLPs have limited expressivity in low-parameter regimes.
AI.method: Proposes QuantumGS framework that integrates Variational Quantum Circuits into Gaussian Splatting pipeline, with unique encoding strategy mapping viewing direction onto Bloch sphere, and replaces classical color-modulating networks with quantum circuits generated via hypernetwork or conditioning mechanism.
AI.result: Achieves higher expressivity and better generalization compared to classical approaches, with source code available for implementation.
AI.conclusion: QuantumGS demonstrates the potential of quantum circuits to enhance neural rendering by leveraging quantum geometry for better representation of view-dependent effects in real-time rendering.

title: Quantum Key Distribution with Imperfections: Recent Advances in Security Proofs
comment: 52 pages; 10 figures; Submitted to the Special Issue "100 years of Quantum Mechanics" of the Brazilian Journal of Physics. Comments are welcome!
summary: In contrast to classical cryptography, where the security of encoded messages typically relies on the inability of standard algorithms to overcome computational complexity assumptions, Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) can enable two spatially separated parties to establish an information-theoretically secure encryption, provided that the QKD protocol is underpinned by a security proof. In the last decades, security proofs robust against a wide range of eavesdropping strategies have established the theoretical soundness of several QKD protocols. However, most proofs are based on idealized models of the physical systems involved in such protocols and often include assumptions that are not satisfied in practical implementations. This mismatch creates a gap between theoretical security guarantees and actual experimental realizations, making QKD protocols vulnerable to attacks. To ensure the security of real-world QKD systems, it is therefore essential to account for imperfections in security analyses. In this article, we present an overview of recent analytical and numerical developments in QKD security proofs, which provide a versatile approach for incorporating imperfections and re-establishing the security of quantum communication protocols under realistic conditions.

AI.tldr: Recent advances in QKD security proofs address the gap between idealized theoretical models and practical implementations by developing analytical and numerical methods that incorporate physical imperfections to ensure real-world security.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to bridge the gap between theoretical security proofs of QKD protocols and practical implementations. While QKD offers information-theoretic security, most security proofs rely on idealized models and assumptions that don't hold in real experimental setups, creating vulnerabilities to attacks. This mismatch necessitates security analyses that account for physical imperfections.
AI.method: The paper presents an overview of recent analytical and numerical developments in QKD security proofs. These approaches provide versatile methods for incorporating imperfections into security analyses, enabling the re-establishment of security guarantees under realistic experimental conditions.
AI.result: The review highlights progress in developing security proof techniques that can handle practical imperfections in QKD systems. These developments offer a framework for analyzing and ensuring security in real-world quantum communication implementations, moving beyond idealized theoretical models.
AI.conclusion: To ensure the security of practical QKD systems, it is essential to develop security proofs that account for physical imperfections. Recent analytical and numerical approaches provide the necessary tools to bridge the gap between theoretical security guarantees and experimental implementations, enabling truly secure quantum communication under realistic conditions.

title: Learning fermionic linear optics with Heisenberg scaling and physical operations
summary: We revisit the problem of learning fermionic linear optics (FLO), also known as fermionic Gaussian unitaries. Given black-box query access to an unknown FLO, previous proposals required $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^5 / \varepsilon^2)$ queries, where $n$ is the system size and $\varepsilon$ is the error in diamond distance. These algorithms also use unphysical operations (i.e., violating fermionic superselection rules) and/or $n$ auxiliary modes to prepare Choi states of the FLO. In this work, we establish efficient and experimentally friendly protocols that obey superselection, use minimal ancilla (at most $1$ extra mode), and exhibit improved dependence on both parameters $n$ and $\varepsilon$. For arbitrary (active) FLOs this algorithm makes at most $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^4 / \varepsilon)$ queries, while for number-conserving (passive) FLOs we show that $\mathcal{O}(n^3 / \varepsilon)$ queries suffice. The complexity of the active case can be further reduced to $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^3 / \varepsilon)$ at the cost of using $n$ ancilla. This marks the first FLO learning algorithm that attains Heisenberg scaling in precision. As a side result, we also demonstrate an improved copy complexity of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n η^2 / \varepsilon^2)$ for time-efficient state tomography of $η$-particle Slater determinants in $\varepsilon$ trace distance, which may be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: Improved quantum learning algorithms for fermionic linear optics with better query complexity, minimal ancilla, and Heisenberg scaling.
AI.motivation: Previous FLO learning algorithms required O(n^5/ε^2) queries, used unphysical operations violating fermionic superselection rules, and/or needed n auxiliary modes for Choi state preparation, motivating more efficient and experimentally friendly protocols.
AI.method: Developed protocols that obey fermionic superselection rules, use minimal ancilla (at most 1 extra mode), and achieve improved query complexity: O(n^4/ε) for arbitrary active FLOs, O(n^3/ε) for number-conserving passive FLOs, and O(n^3/ε) for active FLOs with n ancilla.
AI.result: Achieved first FLO learning algorithm with Heisenberg scaling in precision, with significant improvements in query complexity and experimental feasibility. Also demonstrated improved copy complexity O(nη^2/ε^2) for time-efficient state tomography of η-particle Slater determinants.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes efficient, experimentally friendly FLO learning protocols with minimal ancilla requirements, improved parameter dependencies, and Heisenberg scaling, representing significant advances in quantum learning algorithms for fermionic systems.

title: Near-frustration-free electronic structure Hamiltonian representations and lower bound certificates
summary: Hamiltonian representations based on the sum-of-squares (SOS) hierarchy provide rigorous lower bounds on ground-state energies and facilitate the design of efficient classical and quantum simulation algorithms. This work presents a unified framework connecting SOS decompositions with variational two-particle reduced density matrix (v2RDM) theory. We demonstrate that the ``weighted'' SOS ansatz naturally recovers the dual of the v2RDM program, enabling the strict enforcement of symmetry constraints such as particle number and spin. We provide explicit SOS constructions for the Hubbard model and electronic structure Hamiltonians, ranging from spin-free approximations to full rank-2 expansions. We also highlight theoretical connections to block-invariant symmetry shifts. Numerical benchmarks on molecular systems and Iron-Sulfur clusters validate these near frustration-free representations, demonstrating their utility in improving spectral gap amplification and reducing block encoding costs in quantum algorithms.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unified framework connecting sum-of-squares (SOS) decompositions with variational two-particle reduced density matrix (v2RDM) theory, showing that weighted SOS recovers the dual of v2RDM programs and enables strict symmetry enforcement.
AI.motivation: To establish theoretical connections between SOS hierarchy representations (used for ground-state energy bounds and simulation algorithms) and v2RDM theory, enabling better symmetry enforcement and improved quantum algorithm performance.
AI.method: Developed a unified framework connecting SOS decompositions with v2RDM theory, demonstrating that weighted SOS ansatz recovers the dual of v2RDM programs. Provided explicit SOS constructions for Hubbard model and electronic structure Hamiltonians, ranging from spin-free approximations to full rank-2 expansions.
AI.result: Numerical benchmarks on molecular systems and Iron-Sulfur clusters validate near frustration-free representations, demonstrating utility in improving spectral gap amplification and reducing block encoding costs in quantum algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The unified SOS-v2RDM framework enables strict symmetry enforcement, provides explicit Hamiltonian representations, and improves quantum algorithm efficiency through better spectral properties and reduced encoding costs.

title: Photonic entanglement enhanced multidimensional spectroscopy for probing exciton correlations: theory and applications to photosynthetic aggregates
summary: Nonlinear spectroscopic techniques using entangled photon pairs provide an opportunity to exploit non-classical correlations encoded in two-photon wavefunctions to manipulate two-exciton wavefunctions. We propose an entangled photon pair-enhanced multidimensional spectroscopic technique which is sensitive to exciton-exciton interactions and correlations at the ultrafast timescale. Simulations for a dissipative photosynthetic aggregate reveal the superior ability of entangled photon pairs, compared to both transform-limited and frequency-chirped laser pulses, to manipulate excited-state absorption pathways. The corresponding spectral features in the two-dimensional spectrogram are interpreted in terms of one- and two-exciton resonances. The signal scales linearly with the incoming intensity of the photon sources. It is argued that classifying these resonances using entangled photon source at the perturbative limit allow for probing exciton correlations at the natural energy scale. These insights can be used to explore multi-exciton dynamics using multiphoton entanglement.

AI.tldr: Entangled photon pairs enhance multidimensional spectroscopy for probing exciton-exciton interactions and correlations at ultrafast timescales, outperforming classical laser pulses.
AI.motivation: To exploit non-classical correlations in entangled photon pairs for manipulating two-exciton wavefunctions and probing exciton-exciton interactions at ultrafast timescales, which is challenging with classical light sources.
AI.method: Proposed entangled photon pair-enhanced multidimensional spectroscopic technique using quantum correlations encoded in two-photon wavefunctions. Simulations performed on a dissipative photosynthetic aggregate comparing entangled photon pairs with transform-limited and frequency-chirped laser pulses.
AI.result: Entangled photon pairs demonstrate superior ability to manipulate excited-state absorption pathways compared to classical pulses. The technique reveals spectral features interpretable as one- and two-exciton resonances, with signal scaling linearly with photon source intensity. Enables classification of resonances at perturbative limit for probing exciton correlations at natural energy scales.
AI.conclusion: Entangled photon pair-enhanced spectroscopy provides a powerful approach for exploring multi-exciton dynamics and correlations, with potential applications in studying photosynthetic systems and other complex quantum materials using multiphoton entanglement.

title: Quantum computational imaging and sensing
comment: Appeared in Conference Proceedings Proc. SPIE 12657, Quantum Nanophotonic Materials, Devices, and Systems, 1265703 (2023). Posting here for open access
summary: We present a new framework for imaging and sensing based on utilizing a quantum computer to coherently process quantum information in an electromagnetic field. We describe the framework, its potential to provide improvements in imaging and sensing performance and present an example application, the design of coherent receivers for optical communication. Finally, we go over the improvements in quantum technologies required to fully realize quantum computational imaging and sensing.

AI.tldr: Quantum computational imaging and sensing framework using quantum computers to process electromagnetic field quantum information, with potential performance improvements and application to coherent optical receivers.
AI.motivation: To develop a new imaging and sensing paradigm that leverages quantum computers for coherent processing of quantum information in electromagnetic fields, potentially achieving performance improvements beyond classical approaches.
AI.method: Proposes a framework where quantum computers coherently process quantum information from electromagnetic fields, with specific application to designing coherent receivers for optical communication systems.
AI.result: Presents a theoretical framework for quantum computational imaging and sensing, demonstrating its potential for performance improvements and providing an example application in optical communication receiver design.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computational imaging and sensing represents a promising new approach, but requires further advancements in quantum technologies to be fully realized in practical applications.

title: Quantum Sequential Circuits
summary: This work introduces and characterizes quantum sequential circuits (QSCs) as a hardware-oriented paradigm for quantum computing, built upon a novel foundational element termed the quantum transistor. Unlike conventional qubit-based architectures, QSCs employ symmetry-protected topological junctions where quantum gates are encoded as Choi states via channel-state duality and activated through bulk measurements, utilizing ebits to realize the functional analog of feedback loops in classical sequential circuits. This framework establishes a universal model for quantum computation that inherently incorporates memory and temporal sequencing, complementing existing combinational quantum circuit model. Our work advances the conceptual bridge towards a quantum von Neumann architecture, underscoring the potential of hybrid and modular design principles for the development of large-scale, integrated quantum information processors.

AI.tldr: Quantum sequential circuits (QSCs) introduce a hardware-oriented quantum computing paradigm using quantum transistors and symmetry-protected topological junctions, enabling memory and temporal sequencing analogous to classical sequential circuits.
AI.motivation: To establish a universal quantum computation model that incorporates memory and temporal sequencing, bridging toward a quantum von Neumann architecture for large-scale, integrated quantum information processors.
AI.method: Uses quantum transistors as foundational elements with symmetry-protected topological junctions; encodes quantum gates as Choi states via channel-state duality; activates gates through bulk measurements; utilizes ebits to implement functional analog of classical feedback loops.
AI.result: Develops a universal model for quantum computation that inherently includes memory and temporal sequencing, complementing existing combinational quantum circuit models and advancing toward quantum von Neumann architecture.
AI.conclusion: QSCs provide a hardware-oriented framework for quantum computing with built-in memory and sequencing capabilities, highlighting the potential of hybrid and modular design principles for scalable quantum information processors.

title: Broadband Population Transfer Based on Suture Adiabatic Pulses
summary: High-fidelity coherent population transfer plays a vital role in the realization of quantum memories. However, population transfer with high performance across a broad frequency range is still challenging due to the finite Rabi coupling strength limited by laser powers. Here we propose a novel population-transfer scheme by suturing adiabatic control pulses with each pulse covering certain frequency interval, which are connected in a way that neighboring adiabatic pulses have opposite chirping directions. Taking the widely utilized hyperbolic-square-hyperbolic pulse as an example, we demonstrate that rapid and robust population transfer can be achieved. The transfer bandwidth scales linearly with the number of suture pulses while maintaining high fidelity, even at the suture points where adiabaticity breaks down. Crucially, these pulses can be realized by a single laser by means of temporal multiplexing. For a given bandwidth, this strategy substantially reduces the operational time which is necessary for on demand read-out and suppressing decoherence effects. Our scheme enables a dramatic increase in multimode storage capacity and paves the way for realizing practical quantum networks.

AI.tldr: A novel population-transfer scheme using sutured adiabatic control pulses with opposite chirping directions achieves broad-bandwidth, high-fidelity quantum memory operations with reduced operational time.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity coherent population transfer across broad frequency ranges is challenging due to finite Rabi coupling strength limitations from laser power constraints, hindering quantum memory performance.
AI.method: Suture adiabatic control pulses covering specific frequency intervals, connecting neighboring pulses with opposite chirping directions, using hyperbolic-square-hyperbolic pulses as an example, implemented via temporal multiplexing with a single laser.
AI.result: Achieves rapid, robust population transfer with bandwidth scaling linearly with suture pulse count while maintaining high fidelity, even at suture points where adiabaticity breaks down, substantially reducing operational time for given bandwidth.
AI.conclusion: The scheme enables dramatic increase in multimode storage capacity and paves the way for practical quantum networks by overcoming bandwidth limitations of traditional population transfer methods.

title: Practical continuous-variable quantum key distribution using dynamic digital signal processing: security proof and experimental demonstration
summary: Digital signal processing technology has paved the way for the realization of high-speed continuous-variable quantum key distribution systems. However, existing security proofs are limited to static digital signal processing algorithms, while practical systems rely on dynamic multiple-input multiple-output algorithms to compensate for time-varying channel impairments. Our analysis reveals that the conventional dynamic algorithm, due to its non-unitary nature, systematically underestimates the excess noise, which in turn leads to security issues and the generation of insecure keys. To close this gap, we propose a secure algorithm model, mapping the dynamic algorithm to an equivalent physical optical model whose security can be rigorously assessed. Simulations illustrate the algorithm's non-unitary property and provide a quantitative analysis of the excess noise underestimation caused by the conventional algorithm. We further experimentally validate the necessity of the proposed modeling for dynamic digital signal processing, achieving a secret key rate of 14.4 Mbps based on estimated excess noise of 0.07 shot noise unit; whereas the conventional algorithm would have dangerously overestimated the key rate to 28.2 Mbps with noise of 0.008 shot noise unit. This work provides the essential security framework for dynamic digital signal processing, overcoming a critical impediment for the development of high-performance continuous-variable quantum key distribution systems.

AI.tldr: Dynamic DSP algorithms in CV-QKD systems can create security vulnerabilities by underestimating excess noise, requiring new secure modeling approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing CV-QKD security proofs only cover static DSP algorithms, but practical systems use dynamic MIMO algorithms to compensate for time-varying channel impairments, creating a security gap.
AI.method: Proposed a secure algorithm model that maps dynamic DSP algorithms to equivalent physical optical models for rigorous security assessment, with simulations and experimental validation.
AI.result: Experimental validation achieved 14.4 Mbps secret key rate with 0.07 SNU excess noise, while conventional algorithm would dangerously overestimate to 28.2 Mbps with 0.008 SNU noise.
AI.conclusion: The work provides essential security framework for dynamic DSP, overcoming a critical impediment for high-performance CV-QKD system development.

title: Robust Negativity in the Quantum-to-Classical Transition of Kerr Dynamics
summary: We quantify the quantum-to-classical transition of the single-mode Kerr nonlinear dynamics in the presence of loss. We establish three time scales that govern the dynamics, each with distinct characteristics. For times short compared to the Ehrenfest time, the evolution is classical, characterized by Gaussian dynamics. For sufficiently long times, as we increase the initial photon number, unitary Kerr evolution would generate macroscopic superpositions of coherent states (so-called kitten states), but this is severely restricted in the presence of small photon loss so that expectation values of observables coincide with their classical values. The intermediate time scale, however, shows resilient quantum behavior in the macroscopic limit. We show that in the mean-field non-Gaussian regime, the Kerr Hamiltonian (with small photon loss) generates a significant amount of Wigner-negativity, and classical flow is recovered only if the loss rate grows with system size. Our results broaden the usual understanding of quantum-to-classical transitions and demonstrate the potential for creating robust nonclassical resources for continuous-variable quantum information processing in the presence of loss.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes quantum-to-classical transition in single-mode Kerr nonlinear dynamics with loss, identifying three distinct time scales and showing resilient quantum behavior persists in the macroscopic limit despite small photon loss.
AI.motivation: To understand how quantum-to-classical transitions occur in nonlinear optical systems with dissipation, specifically examining whether macroscopic quantum effects can survive in the presence of loss, which is crucial for practical quantum information applications.
AI.method: Quantitative analysis of single-mode Kerr nonlinear dynamics with photon loss, establishing three distinct time scales: short (classical Gaussian), intermediate (resilient quantum), and long (classical recovery). Examines Wigner-negativity generation and system size dependence of loss rates.
AI.result: Three time scales identified: 1) Short times show classical Gaussian dynamics; 2) Intermediate times exhibit resilient quantum behavior in macroscopic limit; 3) Long times show classical recovery only if loss rate scales with system size. Kerr Hamiltonian with small loss generates significant Wigner-negativity in mean-field non-Gaussian regime.
AI.conclusion: The study broadens understanding of quantum-to-classical transitions, showing that robust nonclassical resources can persist in macroscopic systems despite loss, enabling continuous-variable quantum information processing in realistic conditions.

title: Quantum scattering in helically twisted geometries: Coulomb-like interaction and Aharonov-Bohm effect
summary: We investigate the scattering of a charged quantum particle in a helically twisted background that induces an effective Coulomb-like interaction, in the presence of an Aharonov-Bohm (AB) flux. Starting from the nonrelativistic Schrödinger equation in the twisted metric, we derive the radial equation and show that, after including the AB potential, it can be mapped onto the same Kummer-type differential equation that governs the planar $2D$ Coulomb $+$ AB problem, with a geometry-induced Coulomb strength and the azimuthal quantum number shifted as $m\to m-λ$. We construct the exact scattering solutions, obtain closed expressions for the partial-wave $S$ matrix and phase shifts, and derive the corresponding scattering amplitude, differential cross section, and total cross section. We also show that the pole structure of the $S$ matrix is consistent with the bound-state quantization previously obtained for the helically twisted Coulomb-like problem.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes quantum scattering of a charged particle in a helically twisted background with Coulomb-like interaction and Aharonov-Bohm flux, showing equivalence to 2D Coulomb+AB problem and deriving exact scattering solutions.
AI.motivation: To understand quantum scattering phenomena in curved geometries with both Coulomb-like interactions and topological effects from Aharonov-Bohm flux, specifically in helically twisted backgrounds which induce effective Coulomb potentials.
AI.method: Start from nonrelativistic Schrödinger equation in twisted metric, derive radial equation, include AB potential, map to Kummer-type differential equation governing 2D Coulomb+AB problem, construct exact scattering solutions, derive S-matrix, phase shifts, scattering amplitude, and cross sections.
AI.result: Successfully mapped the helically twisted Coulomb+AB problem to equivalent 2D planar problem with geometry-induced Coulomb strength and shifted azimuthal quantum number m→m-λ. Obtained closed expressions for partial-wave S-matrix, phase shifts, scattering amplitude, differential cross section, and total cross section. Showed S-matrix pole structure consistent with previously obtained bound-state quantization.
AI.conclusion: The scattering problem in a helically twisted background with Coulomb interaction and AB flux is exactly solvable and equivalent to the planar 2D Coulomb+AB problem, with geometry modifying the effective Coulomb strength and shifting the azimuthal quantum number, providing complete analytical description of scattering observables.

title: Gradient Analysis of Barren Plateau in Parameterized Quantum Circuits with multi-qubit gates
summary: The emergence of the Barren Plateau phenomenon poses a significant challenge to quantum machine learning. While most Barren Plateau analyses focus on single-qubit rotation gates, the gradient behavior of Parameterized Quantum Circuits built from multi-qubit gates remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present a general theoretical framework for analyzing the gradient properties of Parameterized Quantum Circuits with multi-qubit gates. Our method generalizes the direct computation framework, bypassing the Haar random assumption on parameters and enabling the calculation of the gradient expectation and variance. We apply this framework to single-layer and deep-layer circuits, deriving analytical results that quantify how gradient variance is co-determined by the size of the multi-qubit gate and the number of qubits, layers, and effective parameters. Numerical simulations validate our findings. Our study provides a refined framework for analyzing and optimizing Parameterized Quantum Circuits with complex multi-qubit gates.

AI.tldr: General theoretical framework for analyzing gradient properties of Parameterized Quantum Circuits with multi-qubit gates, extending beyond single-qubit rotation gates to address Barren Plateau challenges.
AI.motivation: Barren Plateau phenomenon poses significant challenge to quantum machine learning; most analyses focus on single-qubit rotation gates while gradient behavior of circuits with multi-qubit gates remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: General theoretical framework generalizing direct computation framework, bypassing Haar random assumption on parameters, enabling calculation of gradient expectation and variance for single-layer and deep-layer circuits.
AI.result: Analytical results quantifying how gradient variance is co-determined by size of multi-qubit gate, number of qubits, layers, and effective parameters; numerical simulations validate findings.
AI.conclusion: Provides refined framework for analyzing and optimizing Parameterized Quantum Circuits with complex multi-qubit gates, advancing understanding of gradient behavior beyond single-qubit gate analyses.

title: Entanglement-enhanced quantum metrology via alternating in-phase and quadrature modulation
summary: Quantum metrology harnesses quantum entanglement to improve measurement precision beyond standard quantum limit. Although nonlinear interaction is essential for generating entanglement, during signal accumulation, it becomes detrimental and therefore must be suppressed. To address this challenge, we propose an alternating in-phase and quadrature modulation (AIQM) scheme, designed to operate under a fixed nonlinear interaction. During signal accumulation, our time-interleaved approach sequentially applies the in-phase and quadrature driving fields, thereby eliminating the effects of nonlinear interaction on signal accumulation. Our AIQM scheme achieves better metrological performance than conventional schemes, particularly under strong nonlinear interaction and prolonged signal accumulation, with pronounced robustness against parameter variations. By selectively eliminating and utilizing nonlinear interactions via AIQM, our work enables high-precision and high-accuracy entanglement-enhanced sensing without the need for active control of the nonlinear interaction.

AI.tldr: AIQM scheme uses alternating in-phase/quadrature modulation to eliminate detrimental nonlinear effects during signal accumulation while maintaining entanglement benefits, enabling high-precision quantum metrology without active nonlinearity control.
AI.motivation: Quantum metrology uses entanglement to surpass standard quantum limits, but nonlinear interactions essential for generating entanglement become detrimental during signal accumulation and must be suppressed. Current approaches require active control of nonlinear interactions, creating practical limitations.
AI.method: Proposes alternating in-phase and quadrature modulation (AIQM) scheme operating under fixed nonlinear interaction. Uses time-interleaved approach that sequentially applies in-phase and quadrature driving fields during signal accumulation to eliminate nonlinear interaction effects on signal accumulation.
AI.result: AIQM achieves better metrological performance than conventional schemes, particularly under strong nonlinear interaction and prolonged signal accumulation. Demonstrates pronounced robustness against parameter variations. Enables selective elimination and utilization of nonlinear interactions.
AI.conclusion: AIQM enables high-precision and high-accuracy entanglement-enhanced sensing without requiring active control of nonlinear interactions, addressing a key challenge in quantum metrology by separating entanglement generation benefits from signal accumulation limitations.

title: High-order dynamical decoupling in the weak-coupling regime
summary: We introduce a high-order dynamical decoupling (DD) scheme for arbitrary system-bath interactions in the weak-coupling regime. Given any decoupling group $\mathcal G$ that averages the interaction to zero, our construction yields pulse sequences whose length scales as $\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal G| K)$, while canceling all error terms linear in the system-bath coupling strength up to order $K$ in the total evolution time. As a corollary, for an $n$-qubit system with $k$-local system-bath interactions, we obtain an $\mathcal{O}(n^{k-1}K)$-pulse sequence, a significant improvement over existing schemes with $\mathcal{O}(\exp(n))$ pulses (for $k=\mathcal{O}(1)$). The construction is obtained via a mapping to the continuous necklace-splitting problem, which asks how to cut a multi-colored interval into pieces that give each party the same share of every color. We provide explicit pulse sequences for suppressing general single-qubit decoherence, prove that the pulse count is asymptotically optimal, and verify the predicted error scaling in numerical simulations. For the same number of pulses, we observe that our sequences outperform the state-of-the-art Quadratic DD in the weak-coupling regime. We also note that the same construction extends to suppress slow, time-dependent Hamiltonian noise.

AI.tldr: High-order dynamical decoupling scheme using necklace-splitting mapping achieves O(|G|K) pulse sequences for arbitrary system-bath interactions, significantly improving over exponential pulse counts for n-qubit systems.
AI.motivation: Existing dynamical decoupling schemes for arbitrary system-bath interactions require exponentially many pulses in system size, which is impractical for large quantum systems. There's a need for more efficient pulse sequences that can suppress decoherence with polynomial scaling.
AI.method: The method maps the pulse sequence construction problem to the continuous necklace-splitting problem, which involves cutting a multi-colored interval into pieces that give each party equal shares of every color. This mapping yields pulse sequences whose length scales as O(|G|K), where G is the decoupling group and K is the error cancellation order.
AI.result: For n-qubit systems with k-local system-bath interactions, the scheme achieves O(n^{k-1}K)-pulse sequences, a polynomial improvement over existing O(exp(n)) schemes. Explicit pulse sequences are provided for suppressing general single-qubit decoherence, with proven asymptotic optimality and numerical verification of error scaling. The sequences outperform state-of-the-art Quadratic DD in the weak-coupling regime.
AI.conclusion: The necklace-splitting mapping provides an efficient framework for constructing high-order dynamical decoupling sequences with polynomial scaling in system size, offering significant practical advantages for quantum error suppression in the weak-coupling regime. The approach also extends to suppressing slow, time-dependent Hamiltonian noise.

title: Matchgate synthesis via Clifford matchgates and $T$ gates
summary: Matchgate unitaries are ubiquitous in quantum computation due to their relation to non-interacting fermions and because they can be used to benchmark quantum computers. Implementing such unitaries on fault-tolerant devices requires first compiling them into a discrete universal gate set, typically Clifford$+T$. Here, we propose a different approach for their synthesis: compile matchgate unitaries using only matchgate gates. To this end, we first show that the matchgate-Clifford group (the intersection of the matchgate and Clifford groups) plus the $\overline{T}$ gate (a $T$ unitary up to a phase) is universal for the matchgate group. Our approach leverages the connection between $n$-qubit matchgate circuits and the standard representation of $\mathbb{SO}(2n)$, which reduces the compilation from $2^n\times 2^n$ unitaries to $2n\times2n$ ones, thus reducing exponentially the size of the target matrix. Moreover, we rigorously show that this scheme is efficient, as an approximation error $\varepsilon_{\mathbb{SO}(2n)}$ incurred in this smaller-dimensional representation translates at most into an $O(n \,\varepsilon_{\mathbb{SO}(2n)})$ error in the exponentially large unitary. In addition, we study the exact version of the matchgate synthesis problem, and we prove that all matchgate unitaries $U$ such that $U\otimes U^*$ has entries in the ring $\mathbb{Z}\big[1/\sqrt 2,i\big]$ can be exactly synthesized by a finite sequence of gates from the matchgate-Clifford$+\overline{T}$ set, without ancillas. We then use this insight to map optimal exact matchgate synthesis to Boolean satisfiability, and compile the circuits that diagonalize the free-fermionic $XX$ Hamiltonian on $n=4,\,8$ qubits.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel compilation approach for matchgate unitaries using only matchgate gates, showing that matchgate-Clifford + $\overline{T}$ is universal for matchgate group, with efficient synthesis via SO(2n) representation and exact synthesis via Boolean satisfiability.
AI.motivation: Matchgate unitaries are important for quantum computation due to their connection to non-interacting fermions and benchmarking, but implementing them on fault-tolerant devices requires compilation into discrete gate sets like Clifford+T. The paper aims to develop a more efficient compilation approach specifically tailored for matchgate unitaries.
AI.method: 1) Show that matchgate-Clifford group plus $\overline{T}$ gate is universal for matchgate group. 2) Leverage connection between n-qubit matchgate circuits and SO(2n) representation to reduce compilation from 2^n×2^n unitaries to 2n×2n ones. 3) Prove efficiency by bounding error propagation. 4) Study exact synthesis using ring $\mathbb{Z}[1/\sqrt{2},i]$ and map to Boolean satisfiability for optimal compilation.
AI.result: 1) Matchgate-Clifford+$\overline{T}$ is universal for matchgate group. 2) Compilation error in SO(2n) representation translates to at most O(n·ε) error in full unitary. 3) Exact synthesis possible for unitaries where U⊗U* has entries in $\mathbb{Z}[1/\sqrt{2},i]$. 4) Successfully compiled circuits diagonalizing free-fermionic XX Hamiltonian on n=4,8 qubits using Boolean satisfiability approach.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents an efficient compilation framework for matchgate unitaries using matchgate-specific gates, reducing exponential complexity via SO(2n) representation and enabling exact synthesis through algebraic methods and Boolean satisfiability, with practical demonstrations on fermionic Hamiltonians.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Deterministic Inference of $k$-Independent Set Instances on Neutral Atom Arrays
summary: Noisy quantum annealing experiments on Rydberg atom arrays produce measurement outcomes that deviate from ideal distributions, complicating performance evaluation. To enable a data-driven benchmarking methodology for quantum devices that accounts for both solution quality and the classical computational cost of inference from noisy measurements, we introduce deterministic error mitigation (DEM), a shot-level inference procedure informed by experimentally characterized noise. We demonstrate this approach using the decision version of the $k$-independent set problem. Within a Hamming-shell framework, the DEM candidate volume is governed by the binary entropy of the bit-flip error rate, yielding an entropy-controlled classical postprocessing cost. Using experimental measurement data, DEM reduces postprocessing overhead relative to classical inference baselines. Numerical simulations and experimental results from neutral atom devices validate the predicted scaling with system size and error rate. These scalings indicate that one hour of classical computation on an Intel i9 processor corresponds to neutral atom experiments with up to $N=250-450$ atoms at effective error rates, enabling a direct, cost-based comparison between noisy quantum experiments and classical algorithms.

AI.tldr: DEM (deterministic error mitigation) is a shot-level inference method using experimentally characterized noise to benchmark quantum devices, balancing solution quality with classical postprocessing cost, validated on Rydberg atom arrays for k-independent set problems.
AI.motivation: Noisy quantum annealing experiments produce measurement outcomes that deviate from ideal distributions, complicating performance evaluation. There's a need for a data-driven benchmarking methodology that accounts for both solution quality and the classical computational cost of inference from noisy measurements.
AI.method: Introduces deterministic error mitigation (DEM), a shot-level inference procedure informed by experimentally characterized noise. Uses a Hamming-shell framework where the DEM candidate volume is governed by the binary entropy of the bit-flip error rate, yielding entropy-controlled classical postprocessing cost. Demonstrates approach using the decision version of the k-independent set problem.
AI.result: DEM reduces postprocessing overhead relative to classical inference baselines using experimental measurement data. Numerical simulations and experimental results from neutral atom devices validate the predicted scaling with system size and error rate. Scalings indicate that one hour of classical computation corresponds to neutral atom experiments with up to N=250-450 atoms at effective error rates.
AI.conclusion: DEM enables direct, cost-based comparison between noisy quantum experiments and classical algorithms by accounting for both quantum solution quality and classical inference cost, providing a practical benchmarking framework for quantum devices.

title: Bell and EPR experiments with signalling data
summary: The no-signalling principle is a fundamental assumption in Bell-inequality and quantum-steering experiments. Nonetheless, experimental imperfections can lead to apparent violations beyond those expected from finite-sample statistics. Here, we propose extensions of local hidden variable and local hidden state theories that allow for bounded, operationally quantifiable, amounts of signalling. We show how non-classicality tests can be developed for these models, both through exact methods based on the full set of observed statistics and through corrections to the standard Bell and steering inequalities. We demonstrate the applicability of these methods via two scenarios that feature apparent signalling: an IBM quantum processor and post-selected data from inefficient detectors.

AI.tldr: Extended local hidden variable/state theories with bounded signalling enable non-classicality tests for imperfect experiments, demonstrated on IBM quantum processor and inefficient detectors.
AI.motivation: Experimental imperfections in Bell-inequality and quantum-steering experiments can cause apparent signalling violations beyond statistical fluctuations, requiring models that account for bounded signalling to properly assess non-classicality.
AI.method: Develop extensions of local hidden variable (LHV) and local hidden state (LHS) theories that allow for operationally quantifiable bounded signalling, then create non-classicality tests using both exact methods based on full observed statistics and corrections to standard Bell and steering inequalities.
AI.result: Demonstrated applicability on two scenarios with apparent signalling: an IBM quantum processor and post-selected data from inefficient detectors, showing how to properly test non-classicality despite experimental imperfections.
AI.conclusion: Bounded-signalling extensions of LHV/LHS theories provide practical tools for assessing non-classicality in imperfect experimental setups where apparent signalling occurs, enabling more robust quantum tests.

title: Single shot distinguishability of noisy quantum channels
summary: Among the intriguing features of quantum theory, the problem of distinguishing quantum channels is of fundamental interest. In this paper, we focus on the single-shot discrimination of two noisy quantum channels using two distinct classes of probes: single-system (product) probes and entangled probes. Our aim is to identify optimal probing state for specific discrimination tasks and to analyze the necessity and role of entanglement in enhancing channel distinguishability. We show that maximally entangled probes are optimal for discriminating two qubit depolarizing channels, with any nonzero entanglement providing an advantage over single-system probes. In contrast, for dephasing channels in arbitrary dimensions, we prove that single-system probe can be optimal and that entanglement offers no improvement, even when the dephasing unitary is generalized. For qubit amplitude-damping channels, we identify distinct noise-dependent regimes in which either single-system probe outperforms maximally entangled probes and vice-versa. Moreover, we demonstrate that non-maximally entangled probes can act as the optimum probe if the noise parameters restricted to certain values in this task. We also present examples of noisy unitary channels for which discrimination is possible using non-maximally entangled probe, while both single-systems and maximally entangled probes fail. We introduce another class of noisy unitary channels for which perfect discrimination is achievable with a single system, while maximally entangled probes are insufficient. Finally, we show that two erasure channels can be optimally discriminated using any pure single-system probe, with no advantage gained from entanglement.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes optimal probe states for discriminating noisy quantum channels, showing entanglement is necessary for depolarizing channels but not for dephasing or erasure channels, with amplitude-damping channels exhibiting noise-dependent optimality regimes.
