AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental problem of distinguishing quantum channels and determine when entanglement is necessary or beneficial for optimal channel discrimination, particularly comparing single-system probes versus entangled probes.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of single-shot discrimination of noisy quantum channels using different probe classes: single-system (product) probes and entangled probes. Examines specific channel types including depolarizing, dephasing, amplitude-damping, noisy unitary, and erasure channels.
AI.result: 1. Maximally entangled probes are optimal for qubit depolarizing channels (any entanglement provides advantage). 2. Single-system probes can be optimal for dephasing channels (no entanglement advantage). 3. Amplitude-damping channels show noise-dependent regimes where either single-system or maximally entangled probes outperform. 4. Non-maximally entangled probes can be optimal for certain noise parameters. 5. Examples where non-maximally entangled probes succeed while both single-system and maximally entangled probes fail. 6. Cases where single-system probes achieve perfect discrimination while maximally entangled probes fail. 7. Erasure channels optimally discriminated using any pure single-system probe (no entanglement advantage).
AI.conclusion: The necessity and role of entanglement in channel discrimination depends strongly on the specific channel type and noise characteristics. Entanglement is not universally advantageous, and optimal probe strategies vary across different quantum channel discrimination tasks.

title: Arithmetic Reconciliation for CVQKD: Challenges and Feasibility
comment: 9 pages, 10 pages. Journal paper, under review for submission
summary: Continuous variable quantum key distribution allows two legitimate parties to share a common secret key and encompasses reconciliation protocols. A relatively new reconciliation protocol, Arithmetic Reconciliation, presents low complexity and has increasing reconciliation efficiency with lower SNRs. In this paper, we obtain reconciliation efficiencies for this protocol in realistic scenarios, by means of estimation of mutual information, and we also present rates for sequence match of secret keys by Alice and Bob. Results show that this technique is feasible and promising to continuous variable quantum key distribution applications.

AI.tldr: Arithmetic Reconciliation protocol for continuous variable quantum key distribution shows promising reconciliation efficiency at low SNRs with feasible implementation in realistic scenarios.
AI.motivation: To evaluate the performance of Arithmetic Reconciliation protocol in realistic continuous variable quantum key distribution scenarios, particularly its reconciliation efficiency at different signal-to-noise ratios.
AI.method: Used mutual information estimation to obtain reconciliation efficiencies for Arithmetic Reconciliation protocol in realistic scenarios, and presented rates for sequence match of secret keys between Alice and Bob.
AI.result: Arithmetic Reconciliation demonstrates increasing reconciliation efficiency with lower SNRs, and the technique proves feasible for continuous variable quantum key distribution applications.
AI.conclusion: Arithmetic Reconciliation is a promising low-complexity protocol for continuous variable quantum key distribution, showing good performance in realistic conditions with improved efficiency at lower signal-to-noise ratios.

title: Reducing the Complexity of Matrix Multiplication to $O(N^2log_2N)$ by an Asymptotically Optimal Quantum Algorithm
summary: Matrix multiplication is a fundamental classical computing operation whose efficiency becomes a major challenge at scale, especially for machine learning applications. Quantum computing, with its inherent parallelism and exponential storage capacity, offers a potential solution to these limitations. This work presents a quantum kernel-based matrix multiplication algorithm (QKMM) that achieves an asymptotically optimal computational complexity of $ O(N^2 \log_2 N) $, outperforming the classical optimal complexity of $ O(N^{2.371552}) $, where $N$ denotes the matrix dimension. Through noiseless and noisy quantum simulation experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithm not only exhibits superior theoretical efficiency but also shows practical advantages in runtime performance and stability.

AI.tldr: Quantum kernel-based matrix multiplication algorithm (QKMM) achieves O(N² log N) complexity, beating classical O(N^2.371552), with practical advantages demonstrated through simulations.
AI.motivation: Matrix multiplication is computationally expensive at scale, especially for ML applications. Quantum computing offers potential solutions due to inherent parallelism and exponential storage capacity.
AI.method: Proposes a quantum kernel-based matrix multiplication algorithm (QKMM) that leverages quantum computing principles to achieve optimal computational complexity.
AI.result: Achieves asymptotically optimal computational complexity of O(N² log₂ N), outperforming classical optimal complexity of O(N^2.371552). Noiseless and noisy quantum simulation experiments demonstrate practical runtime performance and stability advantages.
AI.conclusion: QKMM provides both theoretical efficiency improvements over classical matrix multiplication and practical advantages in quantum computing implementations, making it promising for large-scale matrix operations in quantum-enhanced computing.

title: Simulation of boson sampling with optical feedback
summary: This work presents a theoretical model of boson sampling with optical feedback, in which a subset of the interferometer's output modes is looped back into the input modes. If the bosons are injected periodically into the input modes of the interferometer and optical feedback lines' length match the period of injection, it allows for interference between bosons injected at the consequent time iterations. We propose several methods methods for computing the output photon distributions in both output spacial and temporal modes, including not only standard spatiotemporal mode-unfolding technique, but also the Kraus-operator formalism, and a correlation-tensor-based approach. The two latter approaches help us to reveal that for random interferometers this system evolves to a unique stationary state over time. Because of the existence of the stationary state, we introduce new computational problem \textit{Stationary Distribution Boson Sampling} which appears to be harder than conventional boson sampling problem and contains it as a special case when there are no optical feedback lines.

AI.tldr: Theoretical model of boson sampling with optical feedback where output modes are looped back to inputs, enabling interference between bosons from different time iterations, leading to a unique stationary state and a new computational problem.
AI.motivation: To extend boson sampling by incorporating optical feedback mechanisms that allow interference between bosons injected at different time periods, creating more complex quantum dynamics and computational problems.
AI.method: Proposes three computational methods: spatiotemporal mode-unfolding technique, Kraus-operator formalism, and correlation-tensor-based approach to compute output photon distributions in both spatial and temporal modes.
AI.result: For random interferometers with optical feedback, the system evolves to a unique stationary state over time, leading to the introduction of Stationary Distribution Boson Sampling as a new computational problem that is harder than conventional boson sampling.
AI.conclusion: Optical feedback in boson sampling creates richer dynamics with stationary states, enabling new computational problems that generalize conventional boson sampling and may have implications for quantum complexity theory and quantum computing.

title: Adaptive controllable architecture of analog Ising machine
summary: As a quantum-inspired, non-traditional analog solver architecture, the analog Ising machine (AIM) has emerged as a distinctive computational paradigm to address the rapidly growing demand for computational power. However, the mathematical understanding of its principles, as well as the optimization of its solution speed and accuracy, remain unclear. In this work, we for the first time systematically discuss multiple implementations of AIM and establish a unified mathematical formulation. On this basis, by treating the binarization constraint of AIM (such as injection locking) as a Lagrange multiplier in optimization theory and combining it with a Lyapunov analysis from dynamical systems theory, an analytical framework for evaluating solution speed and accuracy is constructed, and further demonstrate that conventional AIMs possess a theoretical performance upper bound. Subsequently, by elevating the binarization constraint to a control variable, we propose the controllable analog Ising machine (CAIM), which integrates control Lyapunov functions and momentum-based optimization algorithms to realize adaptive sampling-feedback control, thereby surpassing the performance limits of conventional AIMs. In a proof-of-concept CAIM demonstration implemented using an FPGA-controlled LC-oscillator Ising machine, CAIM achieves a twofold speedup and a 7\% improvement in accuracy over AIM on a 50-node all-to-all weighted MaxCut problem, validating both the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed theoretical framework.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a unified mathematical framework for analog Ising machines (AIMs), identifies their theoretical performance limits, and proposes a controllable analog Ising machine (CAIM) that surpasses these limits through adaptive control.
AI.motivation: Analog Ising machines have emerged as promising computational paradigms but lack systematic mathematical understanding and optimization of their solution speed and accuracy. There's a need for a unified theoretical framework to analyze and improve their performance.
AI.method: 1) Establish unified mathematical formulation for multiple AIM implementations; 2) Treat binarization constraints as Lagrange multipliers and apply Lyapunov analysis; 3) Elevate constraints to control variables to create controllable analog Ising machine (CAIM); 4) Integrate control Lyapunov functions with momentum-based optimization for adaptive sampling-feedback control; 5) Implement proof-of-concept CAIM using FPGA-controlled LC-oscillator Ising machine.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis reveals conventional AIMs have performance upper bounds. CAIM demonstrates 2x speedup and 7% accuracy improvement over conventional AIM on 50-node all-to-all weighted MaxCut problem. The FPGA implementation validates both effectiveness and interpretability of the theoretical framework.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified mathematical framework provides analytical understanding of AIM performance limits. The controllable analog Ising machine (CAIM) successfully surpasses these limits through adaptive control, offering a promising direction for improving analog computing architectures.

title: Simultaneous reconstruction of quantum process and noise via corrupted sensing
summary: Quantum processes, including quantum gates and channels, are integral to various quantum information tasks, making the efficient characterization of these processes and their underlying noise critically important. Here, we propose a framework for quantum process tomography in the presence of corrupted noise that is able to simultaneously reconstruct the process and corrupted noise. Firstly, within the Choi-state representation, we derive the corresponding generalized restricted isometry property and demonstrate the simultaneous reconstruction of various quantum gates under sparse noise. Moreover, in comparison with the Choi-state scheme, the process-matrix representation is employed to simultaneously reconstruct sparse noise and a broader range of target quantum gates. Our results demonstrate that significant reduction in experimental configurations is achievable even under corrupted noise.

AI.tldr: Framework for quantum process tomography that simultaneously reconstructs quantum processes and corrupted noise, achieving significant reduction in experimental configurations.
AI.motivation: Quantum processes (gates and channels) are essential for quantum information tasks, but efficient characterization is challenging due to noise. Current methods struggle with corrupted noise that affects both the process and measurement outcomes, necessitating simultaneous reconstruction approaches.
AI.method: Proposes a framework using two representations: 1) Choi-state representation with derived generalized restricted isometry property for simultaneous reconstruction of quantum gates under sparse noise, and 2) Process-matrix representation for broader range of target gates with sparse noise reconstruction.
AI.result: Demonstrates successful simultaneous reconstruction of various quantum gates under sparse noise conditions. Shows that the process-matrix representation handles a broader range of target gates compared to Choi-state scheme. Achieves significant reduction in required experimental configurations even with corrupted noise present.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables efficient quantum process tomography by simultaneously reconstructing both the target quantum process and corrupted noise, substantially reducing experimental overhead while maintaining reconstruction accuracy under noisy conditions.

title: Hamiltonian Benchmark of a Solid-State Spin-Photon Interface for Computation
comment: 10 pages (main text and refs) + 3 pages (appendices); 6 figures
summary: Light-matter interfaces are pivotal for quantum computation and communication. While typically analyzed using single-mode or open-quantum-system approximations, these models often neglect multi-mode field states and light-matter entanglement, hindering exact protocol modeling. Here, we solve the full Hamiltonian dynamics of a solid-state spin-photon interface for three key protocols: the generation of photon-number superpositions, a controlled photon-photon gate, and the production of photonic cluster states. By deriving exact fidelities, we identify fundamental performance limits. Our results reveal that while realistic imperfections severely limit photon-photon gates, they only slightly affect linear photonic clusters and are nearly harmless for photon-number state superpositions.

AI.tldr: Exact Hamiltonian analysis of solid-state spin-photon interface reveals fundamental performance limits for three quantum protocols, showing photon-photon gates are most sensitive to imperfections while photon-number superpositions are robust.
AI.motivation: Existing single-mode and open-quantum-system approximations neglect multi-mode field states and light-matter entanglement, preventing exact modeling of quantum protocols in light-matter interfaces crucial for quantum computation and communication.
AI.method: Solve full Hamiltonian dynamics of solid-state spin-photon interface for three protocols: photon-number superposition generation, controlled photon-photon gate, and photonic cluster state production. Derive exact fidelities to identify fundamental performance limits.
AI.result: Realistic imperfections severely limit photon-photon gate performance, only slightly affect linear photonic clusters, and are nearly harmless for photon-number state superpositions, revealing protocol-dependent sensitivity to imperfections.
AI.conclusion: Exact Hamiltonian analysis provides fundamental performance limits for quantum protocols in solid-state spin-photon interfaces, showing photon-photon gates are most vulnerable to imperfections while photon-number superpositions remain robust, guiding protocol selection and implementation strategies.

title: Investigations on Quantum Correlations and Open Quantum System Dynamics Through Nuclear Spins
summary:
Nuclear spins provide an ideal platform for studying quantum correlations and open quantum system dynamics across diverse areas, including quantum information, quantum foundations, and many-body physics. This is enabled by their long longitudinal (T1) and transverse (T2) coherence times and precise control using radio frequency pulses. In this thesis, I present my work using nuclear spins to explore these themes.
  First, I study temporal quantum correlations quantified by the Leggett Garg inequality (LGI) for a qubit evolving under a superposition of unitary operators. Using a three qubit quantum register, we experimentally realized superposed unitaries and observed LGI violations exceeding the maximal quantum bound of 1.5, indicating enhanced non-classicality. Notably, this superposed unitary dynamics also showed improved robustness against decoherence.
  Next, I investigate Lee Yang zeros, which are zeros of the partition function in the complex plane that reveal thermodynamic behavior near criticality. We proposed and experimentally demonstrated a method to determine the full set of Lee Yang zeros of an asymmetric Ising model using a single quantum probe in a three-qubit nuclear spin register. We further showed that the mutual information between the probe and system peaks at times corresponding to these zeros.
  I then report our study of the quantum Mpemba effect in nuclear spin relaxation, where systems farther from equilibrium can relax faster than those closer to steady state, verified both theoretically and experimentally using NMR. Finally, I discuss our work on entanglement localization and delocalization induced by local interactions, leading to an apparent violation of the quantum data processing inequality. We showed that this violation is only apparent by constructing a completely positive and trace preserving map describing the dynamics.

AI.tldr: Thesis explores quantum correlations and dynamics using nuclear spins, covering Leggett-Garg inequality violations with superposed unitaries, Lee-Yang zeros detection, quantum Mpemba effect in relaxation, and entanglement localization/delocalization phenomena.
AI.motivation: Nuclear spins provide an ideal platform for studying quantum correlations and open quantum system dynamics due to their long coherence times (T1, T2) and precise control via radio frequency pulses, enabling exploration of fundamental quantum phenomena across quantum information, foundations, and many-body physics.
AI.method: Experimental nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) techniques using three-qubit quantum registers; implementation of superposed unitary operators for Leggett-Garg studies; single quantum probe approach for detecting Lee-Yang zeros; NMR relaxation measurements for quantum Mpemba effect; analysis of entanglement dynamics through local interactions and construction of CPTP maps.
AI.result: 1) Observed Leggett-Garg inequality violations exceeding maximal quantum bound (1.5) with superposed unitaries, showing enhanced non-classicality and improved robustness against decoherence. 2) Demonstrated method to determine full set of Lee-Yang zeros for asymmetric Ising model using single quantum probe, with mutual information peaking at zero times. 3) Verified quantum Mpemba effect theoretically and experimentally in NMR relaxation. 4) Showed apparent violation of quantum data processing inequality in entanglement localization/delocalization, resolved by constructing appropriate CPTP map.
AI.conclusion: Nuclear spins serve as versatile testbeds for exploring diverse quantum phenomena, from temporal correlations and thermodynamic zeros to non-equilibrium relaxation and entanglement dynamics, advancing understanding of fundamental quantum behavior and potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Numerical approaches to entangling dynamics from variational principles
summary: In this work, we address the numerical identification of entanglement in dynamical scenarios. To this end, we consider different programs based on the restriction of the evolution to the set of separable (i.e., non-entangled) states, together with the discretization of the space of variables for numerical computations. As a first approach, we apply linear splitting methods to the restricted, continuous equations of motion derived from variational principles. We utilize an exchange interaction Hamiltonian to confirm that the numerical and analytical solutions coincide in the limit of small time steps. The application to different Hamiltonians shows the wide applicability of the method to detect dynamical entanglement. To avoid the derivation of analytical solutions for complex dynamics, we consider variational, numerical integration schemes, introducing a variational discretization for Lagrangians linear in velocities. Here, we examine and compare two approaches: one in which the system is discretized before the restriction is applied, and another in which the restriction precedes the discretization. We find that the "first-discretize-then-restrict" method becomes numerically unstable, already for the example of an exchange-interaction Hamiltonian, which can be an important consideration for the numerical analysis of constrained quantum dynamics. Thereby, broadly applicable numerical tools, including their limitations, for studying entanglement over time are established for assessing the entangling power of processes that are used in quantum information theory.

AI.tldr: Numerical methods for identifying entanglement in quantum dynamics using separable state restrictions and variational discretization approaches, with comparison of discretization-restriction order effects.
AI.motivation: To develop numerical tools for identifying entanglement in dynamical quantum systems, addressing the need for practical methods to detect entanglement evolution over time in quantum information processes.
AI.method: Two main approaches: (1) Linear splitting methods applied to restricted continuous equations of motion from variational principles, tested with exchange interaction Hamiltonian; (2) Variational numerical integration schemes with Lagrangian linear in velocities, comparing "first-discretize-then-restrict" vs "first-restrict-then-discretize" approaches.
AI.result: Numerical and analytical solutions coincide in small time-step limit for exchange interaction Hamiltonian. The "first-discretize-then-restrict" method becomes numerically unstable even for simple exchange-interaction systems, while the method shows wide applicability for detecting dynamical entanglement across different Hamiltonians.
AI.conclusion: Established broadly applicable numerical tools with identified limitations for studying entanglement dynamics, particularly noting the instability of the "first-discretize-then-restrict" approach, providing important considerations for constrained quantum dynamics analysis in quantum information theory.

title: Efficient implementation of arbitrary Hermitian-preserving and trace-preserving maps
summary: Quantum control has been a cornerstone of quantum information science, driving major advances in quantum computing, quantum communication, and quantum sensing. Over the years, it has enabled the implementation of arbitrary completely positive and trace-preserving (CPTP) maps; an important next step is to extend control to Hermitian-preserving and trace-preserving (HPTP) maps, which underpin applications such as entanglement detection, quantum error mitigation, quantum simulation, and quantum machine learning. Here we present an efficient and fully constructive method for implementing arbitrary HPTP maps. Unlike existing methods that decompose an HPTP map into multiple CPTP maps or approximate it using bipartite Hamiltonians with large Hilbert spaces, our approach compiles a target HPTP map into a single executable CPTP map whose Kraus rank is guaranteed to be no larger than the intrinsic rank of the target HPTP map plus one, followed by simple classical post-processing. Numerical results for inverse noise channels used in quantum error mitigation, including bosonic photon loss, confirm substantial reductions in resources and highlight scalability in higher-dimensional settings. Together with our numerical benchmarks, these results validate the efficiency and versatility of the proposed framework, opening a route to broader quantum-information applications enabled by HPTP processing.

AI.tldr: Efficient constructive method for implementing arbitrary Hermitian-preserving and trace-preserving (HPTP) maps using single CPTP map plus classical post-processing, with applications in quantum error mitigation and quantum information processing.
AI.motivation: Extending quantum control from CPTP maps to HPTP maps is crucial for applications like entanglement detection, quantum error mitigation, quantum simulation, and quantum machine learning, but existing methods are resource-intensive or approximate.
AI.method: Compiles target HPTP map into single executable CPTP map with Kraus rank ≤ intrinsic rank of target HPTP map + 1, followed by classical post-processing, avoiding decomposition into multiple CPTP maps or large Hilbert space approximations.
AI.result: Numerical results for inverse noise channels (including bosonic photon loss) show substantial resource reductions and highlight scalability in higher-dimensional settings, validating efficiency and versatility.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides efficient implementation of arbitrary HPTP maps, opening routes to broader quantum-information applications enabled by HPTP processing.

title: Advanced Quantum Communication and Quantum Networks -- From basic research to future applications
summary: Classical communication is the basis for many of our current and future technologies, such as mobile phones, video conferences, autonomous vehicles and particularly the internet. In contrast, quantum communication is governed by the laws of quantum mechanics. Due to this fundamental difference, it might offer enormous benefits for security applications, more precise measurements, faster computations, and many other fields of application by interconnecting different quantum devices, such as quantum sensors, quantum computers, or quantum memories. This review provides an overview of the specific properties of quantum information networks. This includes the interfaces between the classical and the quantum regime, the transmission of the quantum information by physical implementations, and potential future applications of quantum networks. We aim to provide a starting point based on fundamental concepts of quantum information processing for further research on a future quantum internet.

AI.tldr: Review paper on quantum information networks covering classical-quantum interfaces, quantum information transmission, and future applications, aiming to provide foundational understanding for quantum internet research.
AI.motivation: Quantum communication offers potential advantages over classical communication in security, measurement precision, computation speed, and interconnecting quantum devices. The paper aims to establish fundamental understanding of quantum information networks to support future quantum internet development.
AI.method: Review paper methodology: comprehensive overview of quantum information network properties, including classical-quantum interfaces, physical implementations for quantum information transmission, and analysis of potential applications.
AI.result: Provides systematic framework for understanding quantum information networks, covering key components: interfaces between classical and quantum regimes, transmission mechanisms, and application domains for future quantum networks.
AI.conclusion: The review establishes foundational concepts for quantum information processing in networks, serving as a starting point for further research toward developing a future quantum internet with enhanced capabilities beyond classical communication systems.

title: The Quantum Message Complexity of Distributed Wake-Up with Advice
summary: We consider the distributed wake-up problem with advice, where nodes are equipped with initial knowledge about the network at large. After the adversary awakens a subset of nodes, an oracle computes a bit string (``the advice'') for each node, and the goal is to wake up all sleeping nodes efficiently. We present the first upper and lower bounds on the message complexity for wake-up in the quantum routing model, introduced by Dufoulon, Magniez, and Pandurangan (PODC 2025). In more detail, we give a distributed advising scheme that, given $α$ bits of advice per node, wakes up all nodes with a message complexity of $O( \sqrt{\frac{n^3}{2^{\max\{\lfloor (α-1)/2 \rfloor},0\}}}\cdot\log n )$ with high probability. Our result breaks the $Ω( \frac{n^2}{2^α} )$ barrier known for the classical port numbering model in sufficiently dense graphs. To complement our algorithm, we give a lower bound on the message complexity for distributed quantum algorithms: By leveraging a lower bound result for the single-bit descriptor problem in the query complexity model, we show that wake-up has a quantum message complexity of $Ω( n^{3/2} )$ without advice, which holds independently of how much time we allow. In the setting where an adversary decides which nodes start the algorithm, most graph problems of interest implicitly require solving wake-up, and thus the same lower bound also holds for other fundamental problems such as single-source broadcast and spanning tree construction.

AI.tldr: First quantum routing model analysis of distributed wake-up with advice, showing O(√(n³/2^⌊(α-1)/2⌋)·log n) message complexity with α bits advice, breaking classical Ω(n²/2^α) barrier, and proving Ω(n^{3/2}) quantum lower bound without advice.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the distributed wake-up problem in quantum routing models, motivated by the need to understand fundamental limitations and advantages of quantum distributed computing compared to classical models, particularly when nodes have initial knowledge about the network.
AI.method: Develops a distributed advising scheme for quantum routing where an oracle provides α bits of advice per node, then uses quantum routing techniques to achieve efficient wake-up. For lower bounds, leverages query complexity results for the single-bit descriptor problem to establish fundamental quantum message complexity limits.
AI.result: Achieves O(√(n³/2^{max{⌊(α-1)/2⌋,0}})·log n) message complexity with high probability for wake-up with α bits advice, breaking the classical Ω(n²/2^α) barrier. Proves Ω(n^{3/2}) quantum message complexity lower bound for wake-up without advice, which extends to related problems like broadcast and spanning tree construction.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes the first upper and lower bounds for wake-up in quantum routing models, demonstrating quantum advantages over classical distributed computing and providing fundamental insights into message complexity tradeoffs with advice in quantum settings.

title: Assessing the Sensitivity of Niobium- and Tantalum-Based Superconducting Qubits to Infrared Radiation
summary: The use of tantalum films for superconducting qubits has recently extended qubit coherence times significantly, primarily due to reduced dielectric losses at the metal-air interface. However, the choice of base material also influences the sensitivity to quasiparticle-induced decoherence. In this study, we investigate quasiparticle tunneling rates in niobium and tantalum-based offset-charge-sensitive qubits. Using a source of thermal radiation, we characterize the sensitivity of either material to infrared radiation and explore the impact of the infrared background through the targeted use of in-line filters in the wiring and ambient infrared absorbers. We identify both radiation channels as significant contributions to decoherence for tantalum but not for niobium qubits and achieve tunneling rates of 100 Hz and 300 Hz for niobium and tantalum respectively upon installation of infrared filters. Additionally, we find a time-dependence in the observed tunneling rates on the scale of days, which we interpret as evidence of slowly cooling, thermally radiating components in the experimental setup. Our findings indicate that continued improvements in coherence times may require renewed attention to radiative backgrounds and experimental setup design, especially when introducing new material platforms.

AI.tldr: Tantalum qubits show higher sensitivity to infrared radiation than niobium qubits, requiring infrared filters to reduce quasiparticle tunneling rates, with both wiring and ambient radiation identified as significant decoherence sources.
AI.motivation: While tantalum films have improved superconducting qubit coherence by reducing dielectric losses, the choice of base material affects sensitivity to quasiparticle-induced decoherence, particularly from infrared radiation sources.
AI.method: Characterized quasiparticle tunneling rates in niobium and tantalum-based offset-charge-sensitive qubits using thermal radiation sources, investigated sensitivity to infrared radiation, and explored impact through targeted use of in-line filters in wiring and ambient infrared absorbers.
AI.result: Identified both radiation channels as significant contributions to decoherence for tantalum but not for niobium qubits; achieved tunneling rates of 100 Hz (niobium) and 300 Hz (tantalum) with infrared filters; observed time-dependent tunneling rates on day scales indicating slowly cooling thermal components.
AI.conclusion: Continued improvements in qubit coherence times require renewed attention to radiative backgrounds and experimental setup design, especially when introducing new material platforms like tantalum.

title: Quantum statistical functions
summary: Statistical functions such as the moment-generating function, characteristic function, cumulant-generating function, and second characteristic function are cornerstone tools in classical statistics and probability theory. They provide a powerful means to analyze the statistical properties of a system and find applications in diverse fields, including statistical physics and field theory. While these functions are ubiquitous in classical theory, a quantum counterpart has remained elusive due to the fundamental hurdle of noncommutativity of operators. The lack of such a framework has obscured the deep connections between standard statistical measures and the non-classical features of quantum mechanics. Here, we establish a comprehensive framework for quantum statistical functions that transcends these limitations, naturally unifying the disparate languages of standard quantum statistics, quasiprobability distributions, and weak values. We show that these functions, defined as expectation values with respect to the purified state, naturally reproduce fundamental quantum statistical quantities like expectation values, variance, and covariance upon differentiation. Crucially, by extending this framework to include the concepts of pre- and post-selection, we define conditional quantum statistical functions that uniquely yield weak values and weak variance. We further demonstrate that multivariable quantum statistical functions, when defined with specific operator orderings, correspond to well-known quasiprobability distributions. Our framework provides a cohesive mathematical structure that not only reproduces standard quantum statistical measures but also incorporates nonclassical features of quantum mechanics, thus laying the foundation for a deeper understanding of quantum statistics.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a comprehensive framework for quantum statistical functions that unifies standard quantum statistics, quasiprobability distributions, and weak values, overcoming the noncommutativity challenge in quantum mechanics.
AI.motivation: Statistical functions (moment-generating, characteristic, cumulant-generating, second characteristic functions) are fundamental in classical statistics but lack quantum counterparts due to operator noncommutativity. This gap obscures connections between statistical measures and quantum non-classical features.
AI.method: Develop quantum statistical functions as expectation values with respect to purified states. Extend to conditional forms with pre- and post-selection to obtain weak values and weak variance. Define multivariable versions with specific operator orderings to connect with quasiprobability distributions.
AI.result: The framework naturally reproduces quantum statistical quantities (expectation values, variance, covariance) upon differentiation. Conditional versions yield weak values and weak variance. Multivariable functions correspond to known quasiprobability distributions, providing a unified mathematical structure.
AI.conclusion: The quantum statistical functions framework transcends classical limitations, unifying disparate quantum statistical approaches and incorporating nonclassical features, laying foundation for deeper understanding of quantum statistics.

title: Simulation of Adjoints and Petz Recovery Maps for Unknown Quantum Channels
summary: Transformations of quantum channels, such as the transpose, complex conjugate, and adjoint, are fundamental to quantum information theory. Given access to an unknown channel, a central problem is whether these transformations can be implemented physically with quantum supermaps. While such supermaps are known for unitary operations, the situation for general quantum channels is fundamentally different. In this work, we establish a strict hierarchy of physical realizability for the transposition, complex conjugation, and adjoint transformation of an unknown quantum channel. We present a probabilistic protocol that exactly implements the transpose with a single query. In contrast, we prove no-go theorems showing that neither the complex conjugate nor the adjoint can be implemented by any completely positive supermap, even probabilistically. We then overcome this impossibility by designing a virtual protocol for the complex conjugate based on quasi-probability decomposition, and show its optimality in terms of the diamond norm. As a key application, we propose a protocol to estimate the expectation values resulting from the Petz recovery map of an unknown channel, achieving an improved query complexity compared to existing methods.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a hierarchy of physical realizability for quantum channel transformations (transpose, complex conjugate, adjoint), presents a probabilistic transpose protocol, proves no-go theorems for conjugate/adjoint, overcomes impossibility via quasi-probability decomposition, and applies results to Petz recovery map estimation.
AI.motivation: To determine whether fundamental quantum channel transformations (transpose, complex conjugate, adjoint) can be physically implemented as quantum supermaps when given access to an unknown channel, addressing a central problem in quantum information theory where the situation differs fundamentally from unitary operations.
AI.method: 1) Establish hierarchy of physical realizability for channel transformations; 2) Present probabilistic protocol for exact transpose implementation with single query; 3) Prove no-go theorems showing conjugate/adjoint cannot be implemented by any completely positive supermap (even probabilistically); 4) Design virtual protocol for complex conjugate using quasi-probability decomposition; 5) Prove optimality in diamond norm; 6) Apply to Petz recovery map estimation with improved query complexity.
AI.result: 1) Strict hierarchy: transpose is physically realizable (probabilistic protocol), while conjugate/adjoint are not (no-go theorems); 2) Successful virtual protocol for complex conjugate via quasi-probability decomposition; 3) Optimal diamond norm performance; 4) Application yields improved query complexity for estimating Petz recovery map expectation values compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Quantum channel transformations exhibit fundamental limitations: transpose can be physically implemented probabilistically, but conjugate/adjoint cannot be implemented by any completely positive supermap. However, virtual implementation via quasi-probability decomposition overcomes this limitation, with applications to quantum channel recovery protocols achieving practical improvements.

title: Entropy Bounds via Hypothesis Testing and Its Applications to Two-Way Key Distillation in Quantum Cryptography
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) achieves information-theoretic security, without relying on computational assumptions, by distributing quantum states. To establish secret bits, two honest parties exploit key distillation protocols over measurement outcomes resulting after the the distribution of quantum states. In this work, we establish a rigorous connection between the key rate achievable by applying two-way key distillation, such as advantage distillation, and quantum asymptotic hypothesis testing, via an integral representation of the relative entropy. This connection improves key rates at small to intermediate blocklengths relative to existing fidelity-based bounds and enables the computation of entropy bounds for intermediate to large blocklengths. Moreover, this connection allows one to close the gap between known sufficient and conjectured necessary conditions for key generation in the asymptotic regime, while the precise finite blocklegth conditions remain open. More broadly, our work shows how advances in quantum multiple hypothesis testing can directly sharpen the security analyses of QKD.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a rigorous connection between two-way key distillation rates in QKD and quantum asymptotic hypothesis testing via relative entropy integral representation, improving key rates at small-to-intermediate blocklengths and closing asymptotic gap between sufficient and necessary conditions.
AI.motivation: To improve quantum key distribution (QKD) security analysis by connecting two-way key distillation protocols with quantum hypothesis testing, addressing limitations in existing fidelity-based bounds and bridging gaps between known sufficient and conjectured necessary conditions for key generation.
AI.method: Establishes rigorous connection between achievable key rates from two-way key distillation (like advantage distillation) and quantum asymptotic hypothesis testing using integral representation of relative entropy.
AI.result: Improved key rates at small-to-intermediate blocklengths relative to existing fidelity-based bounds; enabled computation of entropy bounds for intermediate-to-large blocklengths; closed gap between known sufficient and conjectured necessary conditions for key generation in asymptotic regime.
AI.conclusion: Advances in quantum multiple hypothesis testing can directly sharpen QKD security analyses, though precise finite blocklength conditions remain open for future research.

title: Thermal-Drift Sampling: Generating Random Thermal Ensembles for Quantum Chaos Diagnostics
summary: Random thermal states of many-body Hamiltonians underpin studies of thermalization, chaos, and quantum phase transitions, yet their generation remains costly when each Hamiltonian must be prepared individually. We introduce the thermal-drift channel, a measurement-based operation that implements a tunable nonunitary drift along a chosen Pauli term. Based on this channel, we present a measurement-controlled sampling algorithm that generates thermal states together with their Hamiltonian "labels" for general physical models. We prove that the total gate count of our algorithm scales cubically with system size, quadratically with inverse temperature, and as the inverse error tolerance to the two-thirds power, with logarithmic dependence on the allowed failure probability. We also show that the induced label distribution approaches a normal distribution reweighted by the thermal partition function, which makes an explicit trade-off between accuracy and effective range. Numerical simulations for a 2D Heisenberg model validate the predicted scaling and distribution. As an application, we compute unfolding-free level-spacing ratio statistics from sampled thermal states of a 2D transverse-field Ising model and observe a crossover toward the Wigner--Dyson prediction, demonstrating a practical and scalable route to chaos diagnostics and random matrix universality studies on near-term quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: Measurement-based algorithm generates thermal states with Hamiltonian labels using thermal-drift channels, achieving cubic system-size scaling and enabling chaos diagnostics on near-term quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: Random thermal states are fundamental for studying thermalization, chaos, and quantum phase transitions, but generating them individually for each Hamiltonian is computationally expensive. Current methods lack scalability and efficiency for practical applications on near-term quantum devices.
AI.method: Introduces thermal-drift channel, a measurement-based operation implementing tunable nonunitary drift along chosen Pauli terms. Presents measurement-controlled sampling algorithm that generates thermal states together with their Hamiltonian "labels" for general physical models. The algorithm uses these channels to efficiently sample thermal states.
AI.result: Proves total gate count scales cubically with system size, quadratically with inverse temperature, and as inverse error tolerance to the two-thirds power, with logarithmic dependence on failure probability. Shows induced label distribution approaches normal distribution reweighted by thermal partition function. Numerical simulations for 2D Heisenberg model validate scaling and distribution. Application computes unfolding-free level-spacing ratio statistics from sampled thermal states of 2D transverse-field Ising model, observing crossover toward Wigner-Dyson prediction.
AI.conclusion: Provides practical and scalable route to chaos diagnostics and random matrix universality studies on near-term quantum hardware. The thermal-drift channel and measurement-controlled sampling algorithm offer efficient generation of thermal states with Hamiltonian labels, enabling previously challenging studies of thermalization and quantum chaos.

title: Quantum Error Mitigation at the pre-processing stage
summary: The realization of fault-tolerant quantum computers remains a challenging endeavor, forcing state-of-the-art quantum hardware to rely heavily on noise mitigation techniques. Standard quantum error mitigation is typically based on post-processing strategies. In contrast, the present work explores a pre-processing approach, in which the effects of noise are mitigated before performing a measurement on the output state. The main idea is to find an observable $Y$ such that its expectation value on a noisy quantum state $\mathcal{E(ρ)}$ matches the expectation value of a target observable $X$ on the noiseless quantum state $ρ$. Our method requires the execution of a noisy quantum circuit, followed by the measurement of the surrogate observable $Y$. The main enablers of our method in practical scenarios are Tensor Networks. The proposed method improves over Tensor Error Mitigation (TEM) in terms of average error, circuit depth, and complexity, attaining a measurement overhead that approaches the theoretical lower bound. The improvement in terms of classical computation complexity is in the order of $\sim 10^6$ times when compared to the post-processing computational cost of TEM in practical scenarios. Such gain comes from eliminating the need to perform the set of informationally complete positive operator-valued measurements (IC-POVM) required by TEM, as well as any other tomographic strategy.

AI.tldr: Pre-processing quantum error mitigation method using surrogate observables to match noisy measurements to noiseless expectations, with Tensor Networks enabling practical implementation and significant improvements over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Current quantum hardware relies heavily on noise mitigation techniques, but standard approaches use post-processing strategies. The authors propose a pre-processing approach to mitigate noise effects before measurement, addressing limitations of existing methods.
AI.method: Find a surrogate observable Y whose expectation value on noisy state ε(ρ) matches target observable X's expectation on noiseless state ρ. Execute noisy quantum circuit, measure Y instead of X. Use Tensor Networks as main enabler for practical implementation, eliminating need for IC-POVM measurements or tomographic strategies.
AI.result: Method improves over Tensor Error Mitigation (TEM) in average error, circuit depth, and complexity. Achieves measurement overhead approaching theoretical lower bound. Classical computation complexity improvement of ~10⁶ times compared to TEM's post-processing cost in practical scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Pre-processing error mitigation via surrogate observables with Tensor Networks provides superior performance to existing methods, with significant reductions in computational complexity and elimination of tomographic requirements.

title: Quantum Approximate Optimization of Integer Graph Problems and Surpassing Semidefinite Programming for Max-k-Cut
summary: Quantum algorithms for binary optimization problems have been the subject of extensive study. However, the application of quantum algorithms to integer optimization problems remains comparatively unexplored. In this paper, we study the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) applied to integer problems on graphs, with each integer variable encoded in a qudit. We derive a general iterative formula for depth-$p$ QAOA expectation on high-girth $d$-regular graphs of arbitrary size. The cost of evaluating the formula is exponential in the QAOA depth $p$ but does not depend on the graph size. Evaluating this formula for Max-$k$-Cut problem for $p\leq 4$, we identify parameter regimes ($k=3$ with degree $d \leq 10$ and $k=4$ with $d \leq 40$) in which QAOA outperforms the Frieze-Jerrum semi-definite programming (SDP) algorithm, which provides the best worst-case guarantee on the approximation ratio. To strengthen the classical baseline we introduce a new heuristic algorithm, based on the degree-of-saturation, that empirically outperforms both the Frieze-Jerrum algorithm and shallow-depth QAOA. Nevertheless, we provide numerical evidence that QAOA may overtake this heuristic at depth $p\leq 20$. Our results show that moving beyond binary to integer optimization problems can open up new avenues for quantum advantage.

AI.tldr: QAOA applied to integer optimization problems using qudit encoding shows quantum advantage potential over classical SDP algorithms for Max-k-Cut on regular graphs at shallow depths.
AI.motivation: While quantum algorithms for binary optimization have been extensively studied, their application to integer optimization problems remains relatively unexplored, creating an opportunity to investigate quantum advantage in this domain.
AI.method: Study QAOA applied to integer problems on graphs using qudit encoding; derive general iterative formula for depth-p QAOA expectation on high-girth d-regular graphs; evaluate formula for Max-k-Cut problem; compare against Frieze-Jerrum SDP algorithm and introduce new degree-of-saturation heuristic.
AI.result: Identified parameter regimes (k=3 with d≤10 and k=4 with d≤40) where QAOA outperforms Frieze-Jerrum SDP; introduced new heuristic that empirically outperforms both SDP and shallow-depth QAOA; numerical evidence suggests QAOA may overtake heuristic at depth p≤20.
AI.conclusion: Moving beyond binary to integer optimization problems opens new avenues for quantum advantage, with QAOA showing promising performance against classical algorithms for Max-k-Cut on regular graphs.

title: One-Way Quantum Secure Direct Communication with Choice of Measurement Basis as the Secret
summary: Motivated by the question of the distinguishability of ensembles described by the same compressed density operator, we propose a model for one-way quantum secure direct communication using finite ensembles of shared EPR pairs per bit and a public authenticated classical channel, where the local choice of one of two mutually-unbiased measurement bases is the secret bit. In this model, both the encoding and decoding of classical information in quantum systems are implemented by measurements in either the computational or the Hadamard basis. Using the quantum wiretap channel theory, we study the secure net bit rates and certify information-theoretic security of different implementations of our model when the quantum channel is subjected to BB84-symmetric attacks. Since no local unitary operations need to be performed by the receiver, the proposed model is suitable for real-life implementation of secure direct communication in star network configurations.

AI.tldr: Proposes a one-way quantum secure direct communication model using finite EPR pair ensembles per bit, where measurement basis choice encodes secret bits, enabling secure communication without receiver operations.
AI.motivation: Addresses the distinguishability question of ensembles described by the same compressed density operator, aiming to develop practical quantum secure direct communication suitable for real-life implementations.
AI.method: Uses finite ensembles of shared EPR pairs per bit with public authenticated classical channel; encoding/decoding implemented by measurements in computational or Hadamard basis; analyzes security using quantum wiretap channel theory under BB84-symmetric attacks.
AI.result: Studies secure net bit rates and certifies information-theoretic security for different implementations; demonstrates suitability for star network configurations since no local unitary operations are required by the receiver.
AI.conclusion: Proposed model enables practical quantum secure direct communication with provable security, particularly advantageous for network configurations where receiver-side operations are limited.

title: Improved Rodeo Algorithm Performance for Spectral Functions and State Preparation
summary: The Rodeo Algorithm is a quantum computing method for computing the energy spectrum of a Hamiltonian and preparing its energy eigenstates. We discuss how to improve the performance of the rodeo algorithm for each of these two applications. In particular, we demonstrate that using a geometric series of time samples offers a near-optimal optimization space for a given total runtime by studying the Rodeo Algorithm performance on a model Hamiltonian representative of gapped many-body quantum systems. Analytics explain the performance of this time sampling and the conditions for it to maintain the established exponential performance of the Rodeo Algorithm. We finally demonstrate this sampling protocol on various physical Hamiltonians, showing its practical applicability. Our results suggest that geometric series of times provide a practical, near-optimal, and robust time-sampling strategy for quantum state preparation with the Rodeo Algorithm across varied Hamiltonians without requiring model-specific fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using geometric series time sampling to optimize the Rodeo Algorithm for Hamiltonian energy spectrum computation and eigenstate preparation, achieving near-optimal performance without model-specific tuning.
AI.motivation: To improve the performance of the Rodeo Algorithm for two key applications: computing Hamiltonian energy spectra and preparing energy eigenstates, particularly by optimizing the time sampling strategy.
AI.method: Proposes using geometric series of time samples as a near-optimal optimization space for given total runtime. Analyzes performance on model Hamiltonian representative of gapped many-body quantum systems, explains analytical conditions for maintaining exponential performance, and demonstrates on various physical Hamiltonians.
AI.result: Geometric series time sampling provides practical, near-optimal, and robust strategy for quantum state preparation with the Rodeo Algorithm across varied Hamiltonians without requiring model-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Geometric series of times offer an effective optimization strategy for the Rodeo Algorithm that maintains its exponential performance while being broadly applicable to different Hamiltonian systems.

title: Improving Ground State Accuracy of Variational Quantum Eigensolvers with Soft-coded Orthogonal Subspace Representations
summary: We propose a new approach to improve the accuracy of ground state estimates in Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) algorithms by employing subspace representations with soft-coded orthogonality constraints. As in other subspace-based VQE methods, such as the Subspace-Search VQE (SSVQE) and Multistate Contracted VQE (MCVQE), once the parameters are optimized to maximize the subspace overlap with the low-energy sector of the Hamiltonian, one diagonalizes the Hamiltonian restricted to the subspace. Unlike these methods, where \emph{hard-coded} orthogonality constraints are enforced at the circuit level among the states spanning the subspace, we consider a subspace representation where orthogonality is \emph{soft-coded} via penalty terms in the cost function. We show that this representation allows for shallower quantum circuits while maintaining high fidelity when compared to single-state (standard VQE) and multi-state (SSVQE or MCVQE) representations, on two benchmark cases: a $3\times 3$ transverse-field Ising model and random realizations of the Edwards--Anderson spin-glass model on a $4\times 4$ lattice.

AI.tldr: Soft-coded orthogonality constraints in subspace VQE enable shallower circuits while maintaining high fidelity compared to hard-coded approaches.
AI.motivation: Improve ground state estimation accuracy in VQE algorithms by addressing the circuit depth limitations of existing subspace methods with hard-coded orthogonality constraints.
AI.method: Propose subspace representation with soft-coded orthogonality via penalty terms in cost function, rather than hard-coded constraints at circuit level. Compare to standard VQE, SSVQE, and MCVQE on transverse-field Ising model and Edwards-Anderson spin-glass model.
AI.result: Soft-coded approach allows shallower quantum circuits while maintaining high fidelity compared to single-state (standard VQE) and multi-state (SSVQE/MCVQE) representations.
AI.conclusion: Soft-coded orthogonality constraints provide an effective alternative to hard-coded approaches, reducing circuit depth requirements while preserving accuracy in VQE ground state estimation.

title: Quantum noise scaling in continuously operating multiparameter sensors
summary: We experimentally investigate the quantum noise mechanisms that limit continuously operating multiparameter quantum sensors. Using a hybrid rf-dc optically pumped magnetometer, we map the photon shot noise, spin projection noise, and measurement back-action noise over an order of magnitude in probe power and a factor of three in pump power while remaining quantum-noise-limited. We observe linear, quadratic, and cubic scaling of the respective total noise powers with probe photon flux, together with a quadratic dependence of back-action on pump photon flux, in quantitative agreement with a stochastic Bloch-equation model. At higher probe powers, additional probe-induced relaxation modifies the spin-noise spectrum while preserving the integrated noise scaling. Our results reveal fundamental, resource-dependent trade-offs unique to continuously monitored multiparameter sensors and establish experimentally the quantum limits governing their optimal operation.

AI.tldr: Experimental investigation of quantum noise mechanisms in continuously operating multiparameter quantum sensors using hybrid rf-dc optically pumped magnetometer, revealing fundamental trade-offs and quantum limits.
AI.motivation: To understand and characterize the quantum noise mechanisms that limit the performance of continuously operating multiparameter quantum sensors, which is crucial for establishing their fundamental quantum limits and optimal operation.
AI.method: Used a hybrid rf-dc optically pumped magnetometer to map photon shot noise, spin projection noise, and measurement back-action noise over varying probe and pump powers while remaining quantum-noise-limited. Employed a stochastic Bloch-equation model for theoretical comparison.
AI.result: Observed linear, quadratic, and cubic scaling of respective total noise powers with probe photon flux, with quadratic dependence of back-action on pump photon flux, quantitatively agreeing with the stochastic Bloch-equation model. At higher probe powers, additional probe-induced relaxation modifies spin-noise spectrum while preserving integrated noise scaling.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals fundamental, resource-dependent trade-offs unique to continuously monitored multiparameter sensors and experimentally establishes the quantum limits governing their optimal operation.

title: Dissipative Dicke Time Quasicrystals
summary: We investigate the emergence of time quasicrystals (TQCs) in the open Dicke model, subjected to a quasi-periodic Fibonacci drive. TQCs are characterized by a robust sub-harmonic quasi-periodic response that is qualitatively distinct from the external drive. By directly analyzing the dynamics of the system in the thermodynamic limit, we establish the existence of TQC order in this system for a wide parameter regime. Remarkably, we demonstrate that this behavior persists even in the deep quantum regime with only two qubits. We systematically study the dependence of the TQC lifetime, $τ^{\ast}$, on the number of qubits and demonstrate that $τ^{\ast}$ increases monotonically with the system size. Our work demonstrates that quasi-periodically driven dissipative quantum systems can serve as a powerful platform for realizing novel non-equilibrium phases of matter.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates the emergence of time quasicrystals (TQCs) in the quasi-periodically driven open Dicke model, showing robust sub-harmonic quasi-periodic responses that persist even with few qubits and exhibit increasing lifetime with system size.
AI.motivation: To investigate novel non-equilibrium phases of matter in quasi-periodically driven dissipative quantum systems, specifically exploring whether time quasicrystals can emerge in such systems and how they behave in different quantum regimes.
AI.method: Analysis of the open Dicke model subjected to a quasi-periodic Fibonacci drive, directly studying system dynamics in the thermodynamic limit, and systematically examining TQC lifetime dependence on the number of qubits.
AI.result: Established existence of TQC order across wide parameter regimes, demonstrated persistence in deep quantum regime with only two qubits, and showed that TQC lifetime τ* increases monotonically with system size.
AI.conclusion: Quasi-periodically driven dissipative quantum systems provide a powerful platform for realizing novel non-equilibrium phases of matter, specifically time quasicrystals, with robust properties that scale favorably with system size.

title: Modeling integrated frequency shifters and beam splitters
summary: Photonic quantum computing is a strong contender in the race to fault-tolerance. Recent proposals using qubits encoded in frequency modes promise a large reduction in hardware footprint, and have garnered much attention. In this encoding, linear optics, i.e., beam splitters and phase shifters, is necessarily not energy-conserving, and is costly to implement. In this work, we present designs of frequency-mode beam splitters based on modulated arrays of coupled resonators. We develop a methodology to construct their effective transfer matrices based on the SLH formalism for quantum input-output networks. Our methodology is flexible and highly composable, allowing us to define $N$-mode beam splitters either natively based on arrays of $N$-resonators of arbitrary connectivity or as networks of interconnected $l$-mode beam splitters, with $l<N$. We apply our methodology to analyze a two-resonator device, a frequency-domain phase shifter and a Mach-Zehnder interferometer obtained from composing these devices, a four-resonator device, and present a formal no-go theorem on the possibility of natively generating certain $N$-mode frequency-domain beam splitters with arrays of $N$-resonators.

AI.tldr: The paper presents designs for frequency-mode beam splitters using modulated arrays of coupled resonators, develops a methodology based on SLH formalism for constructing their transfer matrices, and analyzes various devices while establishing a no-go theorem for certain N-mode beam splitters.
AI.motivation: Frequency-mode encoding in photonic quantum computing reduces hardware footprint but requires non-energy-conserving linear optics (beam splitters and phase shifters) that are costly to implement. The paper aims to address this challenge by designing efficient frequency-mode beam splitters.
AI.method: Develops methodology using SLH formalism for quantum input-output networks to construct effective transfer matrices for frequency-mode beam splitters based on modulated arrays of coupled resonators. The approach is flexible and composable, allowing construction of N-mode beam splitters either natively from N-resonator arrays or as networks of interconnected l-mode beam splitters (l<N).
AI.result: Presents designs for frequency-mode beam splitters, analyzes a two-resonator device, frequency-domain phase shifter, Mach-Zehnder interferometer composed from these devices, and a four-resonator device. Establishes a formal no-go theorem showing certain N-mode frequency-domain beam splitters cannot be natively generated with arrays of N resonators.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a systematic methodology for designing frequency-mode beam splitters using modulated resonator arrays, offering a flexible and composable approach to implement linear optics in frequency-encoded photonic quantum computing while identifying fundamental limitations through a no-go theorem.
